As for the eighth consciousness, when it takes dispersed objects of its own stage as its object, that which is the object of the mind-king (*citta*) is a primary objective realm (*tattva-viṣaya*), while that which is the object of the mental factors (*caitta*) is a solitary reflection (*pratibimba-mātra*).

(The *Tàixián jí* states: "That which is the object of the mental factors is a solitary reflection because they spontaneously respond to karma and evolve in accordance with the consciousness; since their coarseness and subtlety are equal and they lack superior auxiliary conditions, they arise merely from the self-viewing division (*sva-dṛśya-bhāga*) appearing as those [objects].

The five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*) are by nature coarse and active, and thus possess superior auxiliary assistance—namely, the sense organs (*indriya*) that share the same object and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that shares the same object. Through these, the seeds within the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) are struck and activated, causing the manifest aspect-division (*nimitta-bhāga*) of one's own mind to arise.

If the reflected image (*pratibimba*) were produced solely from the seed, it would follow that its manifest aspect (*pravṛtti-lakṣaṇa*) would not resemble [the object]; yet, since it does resemble the seed, it arises separately from the mind. This is the intention of this master: that these five [consciousnesses] are exclusively "solely reflected images" (*kevala-pratibimba*).
The objects apprehended by the five consciousnesses are the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) of their own level; these are "original natures" (*mūla-svabhāva*).

They may also be "images with substance" (*sadravya-pratibimba*), just as the sixth consciousness, when apprehending the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of the past or future, may be a "solely reflected image" and may also be described as an "image with substance. This is because they are perfumed (*vāsita*) [into seeds].

Because seeds produce the essential nature (*svabhāva*). (The *Taixian ji* states: "The objects of the five consciousnesses are truly only objective realms (*vastu-viṣaya*). When the mind relies on what is produced from the fundamental [nature], it is conventionally termed 'with-essence' (*sanimitta*).

Although it is said to be 'with-essence,' its nature is not intermingled; it does not depend on inference but is clearly and directly realized. It arises from its own seeds and does not arise from the aspect (*ākāra*). Because it takes past and future aggregates as objects where no essential nature exists, it is conventionally termed 'solitary-image' (*kevala-pratibimba*).

Yet, because it arises from the essence and seeds of the past and future, and because it perfumes and produces those same types, it is subsumed under 'with-essence. However, because it is produced by the power of discrimination, it is not called an 'objective realm. For example, the reflection of the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) manifested by the Vajra-mind has no manifest essential nature and is thus called 'solitary-image. Nevertheless, because it arises from the dharmatā-seeds of object and wisdom, and because it perfumes its own new seeds, it is also termed [an objective realm]. )

The Master who maintains the theory of "taking a present entity as the objective basis" (*sābhāsālambana*) says: Because the present contaminated [dharmas] (the eight or five categories) take the future uncontaminated as their object, they can perfume the seeds of the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*). If there were no present dharmas of their own kind, those seeds would not be perfumed;

nor is it the case that the contaminated serves as the objective basis for perfuming uncontaminated seeds, because the manifest state (*dṛṣṭadharmika*) and the uncontaminated are mutually contradictory. Furthermore, since the wisdom and other mental factors of the eighth consciousness lack both seeds and a manifest objective basis, they should not perfume [it]. Therefore, it is illogical that the "solitary reflection" (*kevalapratibimba*) produced by the seeds of the mental factors of the *manovijñāna* could perfume the eighth consciousness.

Moreover, if another dharma serves as the objective basis, the seed would be unrelated to it; and since internal dharmas are not shared, they cannot serve as a basis for perfuming. There are three points of convergence: for example, as when the eighth consciousness takes the "meditative fruit-form" (*samāpattiphalarūpa*) as its object.
The objects of the mind and mental factors are exclusively "solely projected images" (*duoying*).

While the objects of the mind-king (*cittarāja*) are of a real nature (*shixingjing*), they may also be described as "images with substance" (*daizhijing*), because the material form that is the result of meditative concentration (*dingguo-se*) transformed by the sixth consciousness takes that [concentrated object] as its substantial basis (*benzhi*). As the *Taixian ji* states:

"The projected images of gold, silver, and so forth, which arise according to what is contemplated in concentration, are provisionally termed 'images with substance' (*dai-zhi*) as the resulting forms arise accordingly. Some say that when a single type of [consciousness] simultaneously produces both the objective field and the resulting form—these two forms being called "images with substance"—this differs from the case within visual consciousness where the image and the substance are produced from distinct seeds and are thus termed "nature" (*xing*).

It is not so because of the object; do not think that the fruit induced by uncontaminated concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*) must necessarily be of a different kind or not be "associated with a real entity" (*sadravya*). Although the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) produced by karma takes another thing as its real entity, since the seeds are not related, it is not called "associated with a real entity. The fruit of concentration is not otherwise, for it is the color-form (*rūpa*) of the object of concentration that perfumes the fruit.
Secondly, regarding the phrase "according to what is appropriate" (*yathāyogam*) in relation to the nature-seeds (*prakṛti-bīja*) and so forth:

this clarifies that among the three aforementioned objects, according to their respective applications, either the natures are the same while the bound-seeds (*saṃyojana-bīja*) differ—such as when one in a lower stage takes the divine eye or ear of a higher stage as an object—or else the bonds... [text continues]
There are cases where the seeds are of the same kind but their realms differ, such as when the five consciousnesses take the five objects of their own respective realms as conditions;
or cases where the seeds are the same but their bonds differ. This is because, when analyzed in terms of the aggregate, there is one dharma, yet when analyzed individually, they are not.

For example, within the aggregate of the eighth consciousness, the objects of the mental associates (*caitta*) are of the same seed as the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), whereas the objects of the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) have a different bond. (As stated in the *Taehyeon-jip*: "What serves as proof?")

Regarding these three types of objects, Master Zhao says that there is no authoritative scripture or correct reasoning to serve as a standard for them. Master Heshang says that the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (73) states: "Furthermore, there are two other kinds of characteristics: those produced from prior conceptualization and those produced from [the] characteristic itself;

these together constitute the 'characteristic accomplished by both. What is the 'image-characteristic' (*pratibimba-lakṣaṇa*)? It refers to that which arises through pervasive conceptualization and appears through resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), and does not abide in its own fundamental nature. The commentary explains: "Produced from prior conceptualization" refers to the characteristic of the perceiving subject. "Produced from the characteristic" refers to the objective realm (*svabhāva-viṣaya*).

"Accomplished by both" refers to the "concrete" (*sadravyaka*) object. The "image-characteristic" is the "solitary shadow" (*kevala-pratibimba*). This is because it is said to arise from another seed and does not abide in its own fundamental nature. Thus, the Master says: "The perceived and the perceiving are definitely produced from distinct seeds and are each separate."

"Because of perfuming (*vāsanā*)," as stated in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*: "That is to say, the seven evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) and their associated [mental factors], along with the images (*nimitta*) and seeing-aspects (*darśana-bhāga*) they transform, as well as their nature (*svabhāva*), realm (*dhātu*), and stage (*bhūmi*)—excluding those that are the fruit of Buddhahood, the wholesome, and the extremely weak or neutral—perfume the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) to produce seeds of their own kind.

Master [Xuanzang] explained: "This treatise speaks of general characteristics rather than detailed particulars. Furthermore, although there are no separate entities for 'nature,' 'realm,' and so forth, they are merely seeds."

The power of the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect) functions as a secondary influence (*paribhoga*) to permeate the seeds of its own nature; thus, the realm of the cognizing seeds is not intermingled.

The Master [Xuanzang] states that while it perceives all things, there is no essence among the hundred dharmas that is not included within mind, for nothing exists apart from form (*rūpa*) and so forth;

therefore, it must necessarily be of a different substance from the *darśana-bhāga*. Since the *nimitta-bhāga* (perceived aspect) manifested when the conceptual mind forcefully perceives non-existent phenomena and the like must necessarily possess four characteristics...

From what source does the self-perfuming seed arise so as to produce a vision? (The *Taixian ji* states: "This is not logical. If there is no objective entity [the object], how could it arise from seeds such as form? If it were to arise from seeds that lack an objective entity, then it would not be a 'shadow' [image].

Furthermore, if there is no objective entity, the shadow necessarily lacks power and cannot [produce anything]. Even if it were to produce a shadow, what fault would there be in its being produced by the nature of things (*dharmatā*)? Therefore, it arises from perfuming to produce a cognition of its own kind.

The commentary says: "The principle here is not exhaustive. How could an Arhat perceive afflictions? If they do not arise from a vision, from what seed would they arise? If they had their own seeds, the Arhat would have to give rise to defiled dharmas because those seeds exist. Since the Buddha perceives saṃsāra and the teachings of the Two Vehicles, yet lacks those specific seeds, these are merely called 'solitary shadows' (*kevala-nimitta*). At that time, there is no production of a subjective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*)."—*Ji*).

The commentary judges that although one thus distinguishes three types of objects to clarify the principle of *vijñapti-mātra*, this does not eliminate the internal aspects (*nimitta*) and the seeing aspect (*darśana*).

If one were to eliminate the internal aspects and seeing aspect, then while the ultimate would be granted, the conventional would be rendered empty; yet if one grants the existence of the internal conventional, one becomes identical to Bhāviveka.
Therefore, although the school of *Vijñapti-mātra* speaks of "consciousness-only," the preservation of aspects and seeing is the correct tenet, excluding [the view of] mere dependence.
To claim that one returns to the essence of consciousness by means of its external characteristics is contrary to the correct principle, and so forth.
Now, in this *Awakening of Faith*, although the mind and mental factors are differentiated, they are all the evolving manifestations of the single mind;

it is said that when the single mind, which is the Dharma-realm, first moves subtly due to the condition of ignorance, it is called the "karmic consciousness" (*karma-vijñāna*), continuing until the arising of coarse grasping and discrimination, which is called "discriminative consciousness" (*vikalpa-vijñāna*).

The functioning consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) arises from the breath of ignorance to produce mental factors (*caitta*) that grasp the distinct characteristics of objects; these are termed "numerical phenomena" (*saṃkhyā-dharma*).

Therefore, the functional capacity of the single mind flows forth to form the dharmas of mind and mental factors, which have no separate intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) but are all manifestations of the single mind.

Just as it is with the subject that perceives, so too is it with the object perceived; although there is a distinction between the substantial essence (*bhāva*) and its reflected image (*pratibimba*), [they are both of the same nature].

Because that which is manifested by the manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*) has no separate substance apart from the manifesting consciousness itself, although the initial stage exists as the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*) to clarify the meaning of *vijñapti-mātra*, the manifested image-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) does not arise from its own distinct seeds. Rather, the perceiving consciousness arises carrying the reflection of that [image].
Thus, by excluding the image-aspect and retaining only the perceiving subject, the meaning of *vijñapti-mātra* is clarified. Nevertheless, even though that perceiving subject...
The enumeration of the mental factors (*caitta*) is distinct from the mental sovereign (*cittarāja*), yet they lack an intrinsic nature apart from it;

for they are admitted to be transformations of that very mental sovereign. Thus, by subsuming the mental factors back into the sovereign, the doctrine of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*) is established.

Nevertheless, there is a distinction between the primary and derivative aspects of the mental sovereign: the seven derivative consciousnesses are all merely the functional manifestations of the primary consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
Because there is no separate substance, the derivative aspects are subsumed into the fundamental to clarify the meaning of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).

Furthermore, this fundamental consciousness is the aspect moved by ignorance; this moved aspect consists of three types of aspects, namely: the aspect of karma (*karma-lakṣaṇa*), the aspect of seeing (*darśana-lakṣaṇa*), and the aspect of manifestation (*nimitta-lakṣaṇa*).
The aspect of manifestation is that which is manifested by the aspect of seeing, and the aspect of seeing is [itself] the aspect of karma.
It is that which is manifested. As for the "characteristic of karma" (*karmalakṣaṇa*), it is manifested by the true mind; outside of the true mind, there is no separate essence or nature.

It is solely the manifestation of the equality of the *tathāgatagarbha*, wherein all other characteristics are exhausted; therefore, it is called "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*). Thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says:

"The unimpaired characteristic has eight aspects, yet even non-characteristic is without characteristic. Furthermore, the treatise states: "As in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, when [the stages] are exhausted..."

"Through the fulfillment of skillful means, there is a single thought-moment of correspondence wherein the awakening mind first arises; yet this mind has no initial characteristic because it is far removed from subtle thoughts.
Thus one perceives the nature of the mind, which is eternally abiding—this is called ultimate awakening. And so forth.

When the characteristics are exhausted and the nature is fully realized, yet the nature follows along with the characteristics in their flux, this is called the Tathāgatagarbha not maintaining its own nature but following conditions.
It is called "consciousness-only" because the eight consciousnesses—the mind-kings and their mental factors—manifest as aspects, perceptions, seeds, and manifestations.

These manifested aspects are the Tathāgatagarbha manifesting in its entirety; although it accomplishes all phenomena by following conditions, its intrinsic nature is fundamentally neither born nor extinguished.
Thus, principle and phenomena are interpenetrated without obstruction; therefore, the one mind and the two truths are both...
Because it is free from obstructions, it is called "consciousness-only. For this reason, in order to clarify the aforementioned meaning within this treatise, it is said:
"Since all phenomena arise from the mind and are produced by deluded thought, all conceptualizations are merely the conceptualization of one's own mind;

the mind does not see the mind, and no characteristic can be apprehended. It further states: "Therefore, all phenomena are like reflections in a mirror, having no substantial essence that can be grasped."

It states, "Attaining the realization that it is but mind, when the false mind arises, all various phenomena arise," and further, the subsequent text says, "From the very beginning, form and mind are non-dual;
because the nature of form is itself wisdom, the essence of form is formless and is called the Wisdom-body (jñānakāya);
because the nature of wisdom is itself form, it is called the Dharma-body (dharmakāya)," and so forth. This clarifies the principle that phenomena and reality are interpenetrating and unimpeded.
To clarify such meanings as these, the Venerable Master Gandhahastin summarized the holy teachings of an entire era and briefly opened ten gates of *vijñaptimātratā*.

First, because both the aspect (*nimitta*) and the seeing (*darśana*) coexist, it is called "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*). (This is the correct doctrine of Dharmapāla, as explained in detail previously.

Second, because the aspect is subsumed into the seeing, it is called "consciousness-only. (This is the doctrine of the Master Prabhāmitra and others. Third, because the number [of aspects] is subsumed into the sovereign [seeing], it is called "consciousness-only. (This is the doctrine of Asaṅga...)

4. Because one returns to the root from the branches, it is called *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). 5. Because one subsumes characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) into the nature (*dharmatā*), it is called *vijñapti-mātra*.

6. Because the transformation of the true [nature] accomplishes phenomena, it is called *vijñapti-mātra*. 7. Because principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*) are interpenetrating and fused, it is called *vijñapti-mātra*.

(These four gates above represent the interpretations of Bodhisattvas such as Aśvaghoṣa and Sthiramati. 8. Because phenomena are fused and mutually enter one another, it is called *vijñapti-mātra*; this is because the rational nature (*li-xing*) is perfect and complete.
Fusing [phenomena] without obstruction through principle, phenomena themselves are likewise fused so that they do not obstruct one another; or, one enters all and all enter one without any hindrance.
Therefore, it is called "Consciousness-Only" (Vijñaptimātra). Ninth, because all phenomenal characteristics are mutually identical, it is taught as Consciousness-Only:
since phenomena based on principle are not distinct from each other, and since principle and phenomenon have no difference of "this" or "that," the entirety of phenomena is also [identical].
Because one is all, it is called "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*); because the ten realms are infinitely interwoven like Indra’s net, it is taught as consciousness-only.
This means that within one there is all, and within each of those "alls" there is again one and all.
Since this is so, within a single gateway such infinite layers are inexhaustible; every other individual gateway is likewise so, just as in Indra’s net they are infinitely layered.

All manifested appearances are the mind-consciousness, for the *dharmatā* of the Tathāgatagarbha is perfectly interfused; thus, these phenomenal characteristics are rendered thus unimpeded, as explained at length in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

(The above three sections clarify the *vijñaptimātratā* principle of the distinct teaching (*pṛthag-deśanā*) of the *Avataṃsaka*, which is not the primary tenet of the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda Śāstra*).
These ten sections on *vijñaptimātratā* fully cite the sacred teachings and are extensively correlated with various schools, as detailed in the *Ten Sections on Vijñaptimātratā*.
Question: Do the various mental factors (*caitta*) that manifest as images, as asserted by the various masters of the treatises, each have their own distinct essential nature (*svabhāva*)? Answer:
If one follows the *Huayan tantuan ji* (Record of Investigations into the Profundities of the Avataṃsaka) by Xiangxiang, there are four propositions in total:

first, there is only the essential nature without a manifested image, such as in the teachings of the Hīnayāna, because they do not accept the transformation and manifestation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*). Most masters of the treatises, such as Dharmatrāta and others, establish this position.

Regarding this meaning: (1) Although the Hīnayāna does not at all speak of the absence of images (*nimitta*), it simply does not state that the *bhāga* (objective aspect) is called the "mode of activity" (*ākāra*), because it has not yet taught *vijñapti-mātratā* (consciousness-only);
(2) both are real and both are images, as established by the masters of the Initial Teaching of the Mahāyāna and the master Dharmapāla;
(3) there are only images and no real [basis], as established by the masters of the Final Teaching of the Mahāyāna such as Nāgamitra and Sthiramati; (4) neither... [is the case].
This is fundamentally not like a shadow, as in the Mahāyāna Sudden Teaching (Dun-jiao) and the schools of Nāgārjuna and others, which frequently establish this principle. Question:

Regarding the intent of the *Awakening of Faith* (*Qǐxìn lùn*), among the ten gates of Consciousness-Only (*Vijñaptimātra*) and these four propositions (*caturkoṭi*), which Consciousness-Only is taught as the primary tenet of the treatise?

Answer: If one discusses only the "One Mind" and its "Two Gates," one takes the first seven of the ten gates as supplementary; however, if one includes all of them, then the entire set of ten gates constitutes the tenet.
Among the four propositions, the latter three constitute the tenet (*siddhānta*) of this treatise.

If one takes the tenet of the treatise strictly, it is the middle four gates among the ten gates, and within those four propositions, it is specifically the tenet of "only the reflection, no original" (*pratibimba-mātra na mūla*). Question:
How is it known that the tenet of this treatise possesses both a provisional and a definitive aspect? Answer: The compiler states that the single mind-dharmadhātu is free from stillness.

Its nature is characterized by the departure from movement, and its nature is characterized by the departure from stillness. Because it moves to produce the myriad phenomena, and because it departs from the nature of movement, it is originally quiescent.

Yet, because it moves to produce the myriad phenomena, it flows forth to form the differentiated dharmas of the *ālayavijñāna* and other mind-kings (*citta-rāja*) and mental factors (*caitta*), as well as the differentiated objects such as the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) and the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*). These differentiated objects are one.

Because they are manifestations of the mind, when contrasted with the mirror of the one mind, they are the reflections of that single mirror; this is called the "universal reflection" (*sāmānya-chāyā*).
When contrasted with the eight consciousnesses that flow forth from the one mind, they are called the "particular reflections" (*viśeṣa-chāyā*).

For example, the reflections cast by a single round mirror are called the "reflections of one mirror" when viewed in relation to that one mirror, yet each is viewed differently in relation to its respective conditions.

This is called the "pillar-shadow" analogy and other such distinct categories. Regarding shadows, because they possess distinct characteristics, the shadow transformed by the ālayavijñāna serves as the substantial object (*ālambana*), acting as the remote objective condition;

the shadow transformed by the seven consciousnesses serves as the image-object, acting as the immediate objective condition. Thus, the objects of the mind and its mental factors each have both immediate and remote aspects:
the substantial object is the actual entity, while that which is separated from the seeing-part of the evolving consciousnesses is the [remote] object.

The seeing aspect of consciousness (*vijñāna*) is not a transformation of the *ālaya-vijñāna*, yet because it does not exist apart from the object perceived by the seven [evolving] consciousnesses, both the image-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the seeing-aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) coexist;
this is how the meaning of "consciousness-only" (*vijñapti-mātra*) is established. This is the doctrine proclaimed by the Master Dharmapāla.

However, while the images in the specific gate (*viśeṣa-mukha*) are distinct, in the general gate (*sāmānya-mukha*) they are entirely devoid of intrinsic characteristics (*sva-lakṣaṇa*); they are merely a single-flavored image manifested within the one mind.

Because the images perceived through the specific gateways appear distinct from one another, the images of the specific gateways take the images of the universal gateway as their own substance (*svabhāva*).

The images of the universal gateway, in turn, take the fundamental essence of the *ālayavijñāna* as their intrinsic nature. Just as the images of the specific gateways relate to the seven evolving consciousnesses, so it is likewise here.
Taking "seeing" as the substance is like the analogy of looking into a vessel of oil: when the face is white, its reflection appears black.
The seeing is likewise; the seeing follows conditions and merely resembles the appearance of form. By discarding the appearance and returning to the seeing, consciousness alone is revealed.

When the seeds from which both appearance and seeing arise are not [further] differentiated, they illuminate themselves. Masters such as Prajñākaragupta held that while the objective aspect (nimittabhāga) is empty, the subjective aspect (darśanabhāga) is real, and thus attained this principle.
It is not only that the reflected images transformed by the mind do not differ from the substance of the mind; the mind itself—

Since the objects of phenomena are also the objects of the mind-king (*cittarāja*) and possess no separate substance, the mental factors (*caitta*) are subsumed under the king to clarify the principle of *vijñapti-mātratā*.
Thus, the fifth chapter of the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*, in the "Chapter on Seeking," states: "Various radiances of the mind arise as such various aspects;
because the essence of these radiances is neither existent nor non-existent, that phenomenon cannot be apprehended in reality. The commentary explains: "Various radiances of the mind arise."
These various kinds of characteristics are the various radiances of the mind, which manifest as various objective phenomena; they may arise at different times or simultaneously.

Those arising at different times refer to the radiance of greed, the radiance of hatred, and so forth. Those arising simultaneously refer to the radiance of faith, the radiance of diligence, and so forth.
Because the essence of these radiances is neither [substantial] nor non-substantial, one cannot grasp the reality of those dharmas. Such are the mental factors (*caitta*) in their defiled state.

In the state of purity (*viśuddha-bhūmi*), mental factors (*caitta*) possess only the appearance of light but lack the substance of light; therefore, the Blessed One did not declare them to be truly real dharmas.

Since it has already been explained that in the investigation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) and so forth, there is the appearance of light yet no substance of light, by what else could they have as their substance?

It is because the mind-king (*cittarāja*) serves as their substance that they are called "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*); it does not mean that mental factors are simply separate from the mind.
The king has no intrinsic nature, and the seven evolving consciousnesses likewise lack intrinsic nature apart from the fundamental consciousness;

therefore, they are called "consciousness-only. As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "The ocean of the storehouse-consciousness is ever-present, stirred by the winds of objective spheres, so that the various waves of consciousness surge and arise.
Even their distinctness cannot be found; for how could there be separate waves apart from the water? The same applies to the seven consciousnesses.

Reflect upon this accordingly: not only do the seven consciousnesses not exist apart from the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), but even the characteristics of the fundamental consciousness itself are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature when separated from the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Because it is *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* states: "The pure *tathāgatagarbha* is the worldly *ālayavijñāna*;
like gold fashioned into a finger-ring, they are mutually indistinguishable. This metaphor should be explained in accordance with the Dharma.
The *Dhātunirviśeṣa-śāstra* and the *Gandhahastin-ṭīkā* collectively clarify the principles of the depth and shallowness of this very *vijñapti-mātra*.
The treatise states: "Based on the single dharma of the One Mind, there are two gates: first, the gate of the True Suchness of Mind; second, the gate of the Arising and Ceasing of Mind.
These two gates each encompass all mundane and supramundane dharmas. By means of these two gates...

Because they are not dissociated, and so forth; the other gates are as previously asked. Regarding the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) of the thesis, the position that "only the reflection exists and the original object does not" is the primary tenet of this treatise.
The reflection transformed by the mind that acts as the perceiving subject takes that very mind as its substantial basis (*upādāna*).
For example, the reflection in an oil-filled bowl takes the face as its substantial basis. How could it be that only the reflection lacks a basis? [The answer is: All things.
Since sentient beings and the Tathāgata are both shadows manifested by the single mind, it is said that "there is only consciousness and no objective substance.
Thus, the treatise states: "That which is seen by the minds of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles is called the response-body (nirmāṇakāya).

Because they do not know that it is manifested by the evolving consciousnesses, they see it as coming from outside; they grasp at its physical dimensions and cannot fully comprehend it. Furthermore, the *Mahā-avaivarta-sūtra* (Great Ornament Sūtra) says:
It is said that one should see for oneself that the Buddhas of the future will place their hands upon one's head and preach the Dharma; this distinct practice of body and mind is inconceivable.
Furthermore, a verse from the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says:
"If anyone wishes to know all the Buddhas of the three periods of time, they should contemplate in this manner."
Regarding the statement that "the mind creates all Tathāgatas," even within the Hīnayāna it is taught that mental images are called "aspects" (*ākāra*).

These are subsumed within the mind, just as reflections in a mirror are subsumed by the mirror. How could it be that there are no images at all? [The opponent] replies: Although they are called "aspects," they do not...

The *Chengxiang fen* (Chapter on the Characteristics) is said to be "without images" (*wuying*) because it has not yet clarified the principle of the manifestation of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*); one should reflect upon this accordingly.

Fifth, regarding the establishment of the gates of similarity and difference in perfuming (*vāsanā*):

according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, only that which is fully endowed with four characteristics constitutes the perfumable (*bhāvyamāna*), and only that which is fully endowed with four characteristics constitutes the perfumer (*bhāvaka*).

Furthermore, only that which is fully endowed with six characteristics constitutes the seed of perfuming. Because it must be fully endowed with four characteristics to constitute the perfumable, the resultant mind-king (*vipākacitta*) serves as the perfumable.
It is not that the three natures, the seven consciousnesses, and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) also possess the four conditions to constitute the perfuming agent (*bhāvakatva*);

rather, only the three natures and the seven consciousnesses—specifically their *darśana* (seeing) and *nimitta* (image) aspects—constitute the perfuming agent. This excludes the ripening consciousness (*vipākacitta*) and suchness (*tathatā*).

Regarding the four conditions for being the perfumed object (*bhāvyatva*), as stated in the second chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*: first, the quality of stable persistence; if a phenomenon remains of one kind from beginning to end...

That which is capable of maintaining habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) through continuity is what is perfumed (*bhāvya*). This excludes the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), as well as sound, wind, and so forth, because their nature is not stable and thus they are not perfumable.
Second, regarding the two types of neutral (*avyākṛta*) natures: if a dharma is impartial and free from contradiction, it can contain habitual tendencies and is thus perfumable;
however, because wholesome and defiled states possess powerful force, they cannot accommodate [neutral seeds] and are therefore not perfumable.

1. Regarding perfuming (*vāsanā*), by virtue of this, the eighth pure consciousness (*viśuddha-vijñāna*) of the Tathāgata carries only pre-existing seeds and does not receive new perfuming. 2. Third, regarding the nature of being perfumable:
if a phenomenon possesses sovereignty, its nature is not firm and dense, and it can receive habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), then it is a perfumable object (*bhāvya*).

This excludes mental factors (*caitta*) and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), because they lack dependence on others and lack firm density, and thus are not perfumable. 3. Fourth, it must be in conjunction with the perfuming agent (*bhāvaka*).

If the nature [of the *ālayavijñāna*] exists simultaneously with and in the same location as the perfuming agent (*vāsaka*), being neither separate from nor identical to it, then it is that which is perfumed (*bhāvya*).
This excludes the possibility of other bodies or moments preceding and following [the *ālayavijñāna*], as they lack the meaning of conjunction; therefore, they are not what is perfumed.

Only the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) possesses these four conditions and can be the perfumable, whereas those seven consciousnesses and so forth do not possess these four conditions and are therefore not the perfumable. Question: With regard to...?

Regarding the eighth question: "Are the five categories of mental factors associated with [the storehouse consciousness] both that which is perfumed (*bhāvyamāna*) and that which perfumes (*bhāvaka*)?
Answer: There is a dispute among the masters of the Western regions. One master, the Ācārya Nanda, says: "Mental factors are also perfumed in the same manner as the sovereign mind-king (*cittarāja*);

for the verse also states 'likewise' (*tathā*), meaning they both follow the sovereign mind-king. It is only the eighth mind-king that is designated as the object of perfuming within the sacred teachings."

The second Dharma-protector master (Dharmapāla) says: although the mind (*citta*) is that which is perfumed (*bhāvya*), the mental factors (*caitta*) are neither perfumed nor are they perfumers (*bhāvaka*).
If one were to allow them to be perfumed, a single sentient being would possess six distinct entities, because there would be six locations of perfuming and thus six types of seeds.
If one were to allow them to be perfumers, they would be the same as the mind-king (*cittarāja*) in being unobscured and neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Question: How can it be said that [the storehouse consciousness] is perfumed? For it does not possess the four characteristics of a perfuming agent (*kṣepaka*).

Question: If that were so, Nanda might raise an objection, saying: "If the seven transforming consciousnesses are all perfuming agents, then since there are distinct seeds from these perfuming agents, how could they be established as a single type?
Dharmapāla explains this: although the perfuming agents are distinct, the perfumable [consciousness] is one; therefore, it is established [as a single type].

The analogy of the single fruit and Nanda states: "I am also like this; although there are six [consciousnesses] that are perfumed, they proceed from the sovereign mind-king as a single seed to produce a single fruit. Such an explanation by analogy is consistent in its reasoning.

However, within the school of *Vijñaptimātra*, the doctrine of Dharmapāla is the correct interpretation. Now, regarding the eighth consciousness, which has four parts (*bhāga*), which part is the primary subject?

Regarding what is perfumed (*bhāvyamāna*), Master Xuánlóng replied: "The self-verifying aspect (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) is precisely that which is perfumed, because it is the substance of consciousness," and so forth.
As for the four characteristics of the perfuming agent (*bhāvakadharma*), they are also as stated in the treatise: first, there must be arising and ceasing;

if a phenomenon is not impermanent, it cannot possess the functional capacity to produce and grow habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). This excludes unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), as they lack such sequential activity.

Because transformation lacks the function of growth and production, it is not a perfuming agent (this differs from the tenet of the *Awakening of Faith*, which explains the meaning of "intrinsic purity" and "non-awakening" as internal perfuming to mean the perfuming of *tathatā*;

this shall be understood in detail below). Second, that which possesses superior function: if there is arising and ceasing, and its power is increased and intensified so as to trigger habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), then it is a perfuming agent.
This excludes the mind and mental factors of maturation (*vipāka*), because their power is weak and inferior, and thus they are not perfuming agents.

(As this also differs from the tenets of the *Awakening of Faith*, the meaning of the perfuming of fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*) and the meaning of the perfuming of the fundamental karmic consciousness (*mūlakarmavijñāna*) will be explained in detail below. Third, regarding increase and decrease:
if there were a superior function capable of increasing or decreasing, that which implants and stores habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) would be a perfuming agent (*kṣobhaka*).

This [perfuming] is excluded because the perfected wholesome dharmas of the Buddha-fruit have neither increase nor decrease; therefore, they are not perfuming agents. If they were perfuming agents, the Buddha-fruits of preceding and succeeding [Buddhas] would not be perfected.

There must be a distinction between superior and inferior [capacities] (which differs slightly from the *Awakening of Faith*, as the perfuming of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is never interrupted and constantly gives rise to sovereign function; thus, the Buddha-fruit also perfumes, as the cited text below shows).

Fourth, it evolves in conjunction with that which is perfumed (*bhāvyamāna*); if it is simultaneous and co-spatial with the perfumable, neither separated nor identical, then it is the perfumer (*bhāvaka*).

This excludes the possibility that the Nirmāṇakāya (Emanation Body) could be the perfumer, because there is no sense of conjunction between its preceding and succeeding moments; therefore, it alone is not the perfumer.

Regarding the seven evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and their associated mental factors (*caitta*), those that possess superior functional power and undergo increase and decrease fulfill these four criteria and may thus be considered "perfumers" (*bhāvaka*).
However, because the eighth consciousness does not fulfill these four criteria, it is not a perfumer. Question:
Are all four parts of each of the seven consciousnesses and their mental factors perfumers? Answer: Some say that all four parts are indeed perfumers.

Because they are both produced through co-activity, and because only that which is the "appropriated" (the subjective) has the status of being perfumable (*vāsanīya*), the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and so forth are not perfumable.
Some claim that all four parts are capable of perfuming; this is incorrect, because the mental factors (*caitta*) do not each perfume their own seeds.

Therefore, it is now established that each of the four parts possesses its own substantial nature (*svabhāva*). It is on the basis of these four parts having their own substantial natures that they are considered the perfumers (*vāsaka*), and not merely as the four [parts] themselves.

Regarding the function of the divisions, the meaning of the "division of self-nature" (*svabhāva-bhāga*) and "self-corroboration" (*svasaṃvitti*) differs slightly [as Master Xuánlóng and others have stated].

Question: Are all four types of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) capable of perfuming (*bhāvaka*)? Answer: The three types—the indeterminate of deportment (*airyāpathika*), the indeterminate of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), and the indeterminate of transformation (*nairmāṇika*)—are definitely capable of perfuming.
Regarding the indeterminate of maturation (*vipāka-avyākṛta*), there are two kinds: first, true maturation, which refers to the eighth consciousness (*aṣṭama-vijñāna*).
Because their nature is weak and inferior, they are not capable of perfuming. Furthermore, the two types of *vipāka-ja* (born of maturation) also have two kinds:

first, the six consciousnesses and their mental factors induced by wholesome and unwholesome karma; because these belong to the category of maturation and their nature is weak and inferior, they are not capable of perfuming.

All other *anivṛtāvyākṛta* (unobscured-neutral) dharmas resulting from skillful means are called capable of perfuming. It is said that the *nivṛtāvyākṛta* (obscured-neutral) perfumes and forms the *ālaya-vijñāna*.
Regarding the seeds of *ya-ji* (the causal basis), as stated above in the section on Consciousness-Only (*Vijñaptimātra*), the six characteristics of seeds are also as the treatise says:

first, momentary destruction (*kṣaṇika-nirodha*). This means that as soon as their substance arises, they must necessarily perish in the immediate interval; only when possessing superior functional power do they constitute seeds.

This excludes permanent phenomena (*nityadharma*), which lack transformation and therefore cannot possess the capacity for productive activity. (This point also differs slightly from the *Awakening of Faith*, which posits True Suchness [Tathatā]...)

The meaning of internal perfuming constitutes the primary cause of Buddhahood; how could it lack the functional capacity to produce [results]? Second, regarding "the coexistence with the fruit": this means that only when it is present and in conjunction with the manifest dharmas—the fruits produced by it—does it constitute a seed.

This excludes [the seed] being prior to or subsequent to the fruit, or being fixedly separated from it. Manifest [dharmas] and seeds, though of different categories, do not mutually contradict one another;
they possess the functional capacity to produce [results] simultaneously within a single body, unlike the case where seeds of their own kind arise sequentially.
Later, they will certainly not coexist. Although causes and effects may sometimes coexist and sometimes not, it is only at the time of the present that a causal function can exist;

for that which has already arisen or has already ceased lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Therefore, the designation "seed" is established based on its production of a present effect, not because it draws forth its own kind.
Consequently, one should simply state that there are three [factors] that always persist together with the cause and the fruit, namely: that which is required...

A seed is established only when a homogeneous continuity persists for a long duration until the ultimate stage; this excludes the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), which are subject to change and interruption, as they do not correspond to the nature of a seed.
This demonstrates that seeds arise from their own kind (*svajāti*) and that their four characteristics are determined:
according to the power of their causes, they produce wholesome, unwholesome, and so forth, functions that are fixed, only then constituting a seed. This excludes [the evolving consciousnesses].
Other schools maintain that there is a causal principle whereby a cause of a different nature produces an effect of a different nature. Regarding the "fivefold dependence on conditions":
this means that for something to constitute a seed, it must depend upon the conjunction of its own specific conditions, resulting in a particular excellence of functional capacity (*śakti*).

This refutes the non-Buddhist (Tīrthika) adherence to a spontaneous cause (*svabhāva-hetu*) that does not depend on conditions yet constantly and simultaneously produces effects; or alternatively, it refutes other schools who hold that conditions are never absent, thereby demonstrating what is [meant by] the "perpetual non-existence" of conditions.
Because it depends on conditions and does not possess a permanent nature, the seed does not produce its fruit constantly or all at once. Regarding the "drawing forth of its own fruit":
this means that a seed only becomes such when it individually draws forth its respective fruits, such as various forms (*rūpa*) and moments of mind (*citta*).

This refutes the non-Buddhist (Tīrthika) tenet that a single cause produces all effects, or the tenet of other schools that form and mind mutually serve as causes and conditions for one another. Only...

Within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), it is only when the differentiation of functional capacities (*śakti-viśeṣa*) possesses these six characteristics that it constitutes a seed (*bīja*); it is not otherwise.
External grains such as rice or wheat are merely designated by the name "seed" because they are transformations of consciousness; they are not actual seeds. Question:

Regarding the various defiled seeds that possess these six characteristics, should one say they are inherently present by nature (*dharmatā-prakṛti-stha*) from the beginning, or should one say they are established through perfuming (*vāsanā*) at a later time? Answer: There is a dispute regarding this in the West (India).
The Master Nanda said: "The seeds of all phenomena are all produced through perfuming (*vāsanā*);

because the principle that causes produce effects is without deviation, it is like flowers perfuming sesame seeds—there is no such thing as [perfuming] not being produced. The principle herein is also like this.

Even if one were to claim that there is a cause existing prior to perfuming, there would likewise be an effect existing prior to the cause. If one says that an effect does not exist, it cannot arise from a cause."
Those who hold that [the seeds] are produced [rather than innate] argue that they arise through perfuming and not otherwise. The master Ratnākaraśānti states:
"All phenomena each possess their own intrinsic nature as a seed, which does not arise from perfuming; it must first exist as a nature before the fruit can exist.
He uses the fire-nature within wood as an analogy for this same principle. Although those perfumed seeds do indeed have an intrinsic nature, they are nonetheless [conditioned by] purity and impurity.
Because it is perfumed and activated by pure karma, the seed undergoes a transformation such that it acquires the capacity to produce a fruit;
yet this new black [karma] does not produce a separate seed, for it is simply that original nature which serves as the seed.

Although these seeds are non-dual and undifferentiated, two types are established based on their preceding and succeeding states: that which exists prior to being perfumed is called the "abiding in its own nature" (*svabhāva-vihita*).
After the realms (*dhātu*) have been perfumed and activated, they are said to be "increased through habituation" (*vāsanā-vṛddhi*).
Since the realm does not depend on perfuming yet exists as a cause beforehand, nor does it sustain a cause, the effect would likewise have to exist beforehand. This point is admitted by both parties.

Just as a cause that does not sustain perfuming exists as a causal nature beforehand and later becomes a causal event upon depending on the perfuming of an object, so too [the effect] would exist as a resultant nature beforehand, independent of the time of the cause, and later depend [on it].
That phenomenon is established by means of its cause; yet, as for this duality of cause and effect, neither has yet fulfilled its functional efficacy.
Therefore, they are collectively termed "intrinsic nature seeds" (*prakṛti-bīja*). As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The cause is itself the fruit;
when the fruit increases, it becomes functional. Good son, although there will be retribution in future ages, because it has not yet been received, it is designated as such."
The cause and the time of its reception—this is called "increase. By this principle, the previous objection can be resolved.

If it were said that there is no original nature-seed (*prakṛti-bīja*) but that causes are produced solely through the perfuming of designations (*nāma-vyavahāra*), then even phenomena such as rabbit horns would have to arise, because they too would have the perfuming of designations as their cause. Therefore, the Master Dharmapāla stated that there are two types of seeds.
This refers to newly perfumed seeds (*navābhyāsabīja*) and innate seeds (*prakṛtisthabīja*). One must possess both of these [types of seeds] for a fruit to arise.
Just as there are two kinds of seeds within defiled phenomena (*saṃkliṣṭadharma*), it should be known that pure phenomena (*viśuddhadharma*) likewise have two kinds.

However, regarding pure phenomena, it is only when the newly perfumed seeds reach the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the first untainted (*anāsrava*) state arises that they can be fully perfumed. From this point upward, the three factors proceed simultaneously and in parallel.
"Arising" refers to the newly produced manifest uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomena, the innate seeds (*dharmatā-bīja*), and the newly perfumed seeds produced by these manifest phenomena.
Question: Among these three factors, upon which factor is the "noble nature" (*āryatva*) metaphorically established?
Answer: It is metaphorically established upon the newly produced manifest uncontaminated phenomena and the innate seeds. If one sees...
If [the designation "holy"] were established based on seeds that exist as the natural state (*dharmatā*) prior to the Path, then ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) would also have to be called holy.
If it were established based on newly perfumed seeds, one could not call those in the first moment [of the Path] holy.

If it were established based on active manifestations (*samudācāra*), one could not call those in the state of emerging from meditative absorption holy, because their outflow-free state is interrupted and mixed with outflows. Therefore, this is not the case for those from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward.

Therefore, because the person (*pudgala*) is empty and there is a continuity of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), it is merely comprised of the three kinds of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) which contain the seeds for the arising of the outflowing (*sāsrava*).

Regarding these three kinds of habitual tendencies, as stated in the eighth chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*: "The first is the habitual tendency of names and words (*nāma-pada-vāsanā*), meaning that each conditioned phenomenon has its own distinct direct seed.
There are two kinds of names and words: first, names and words that express meaning (*artha-vyañjana-nāma-pada*), which refers to the expressive [words]."
The distinctions between the two types of objective designations (*nāma*) and verbal expressions (*abhilāpa*) are as follows:

first, the seeds perfumed by these two types of designations—which serve as the specific causes and conditions for each conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*)—consist of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) that apprehend objects;

second, the habitual tendencies of the two forms of self-grasping (*ātma-grāha-vāsanā*), which are the seeds of the false attachment to "self" and "mine. These [tendencies] are of two kinds: (1) innate (*sahaja*) and (2) conceptually constructed (*vikalpita*). These follow the two types of self-grasping.
The seeds perfumed by grasping (*upādāna*) cause the distinctions between self and others among sentient beings; these are the latencies of the members of existence (*bhavāṅga-vāsanā*).
This refers to the karmic seeds that summon the retribution of the three realms. These are of two types: first, contaminated wholesome karma, and second, unwholesome karma.

One should understand that the seeds perfumed by these two types of karma cause the distinctions in the retributions of the six destinies. Furthermore, there are the latencies of the members of existence associated with the grasping of a self (*ātma-grāha*).

Regarding the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for differentiated fruits: a question is asked whether these three types of latencies (*vāsanā*) consist solely of *sāsrava* (contaminated) seeds, or if they also include *anāsrava* (uncontaminated) seeds.
The answer is that our teacher says: some maintain that uncontaminated seeds are subsumed under the perfuming of names and words (*nāma-vyañjana-vāsanā*);
others maintain that uncontaminated seeds are not subsumed under these three types of perfuming. Thus, there are three [positions].

The perfuming (vāsanā) is spoken of in terms of the contaminated (sāsrava). This is because all contaminated phenomena are pursued by the latent tendencies of linguistic designation (nāma-kilbiṣa-anuśaya);
due to the distinctions in the perfuming of linguistic designations, they are so. The uncontaminated (anāsrava) is not like this;

it arises directly through the power of repeated cultivation of subsequently attained wisdom (pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna), which establishes distinctions such as [the stages of] the path. Furthermore, these distinctions arise from the very nature of reality (dharmatā).

The detailed explanation of the characteristics of the three types of perfuming (*vāsanā*) in relation to the eight consciousnesses and the eleven consciousnesses—including the world and so forth—is to be found in the *Daśamukha-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Ten-Gate Treatise on Consciousness-Only).
(In the *Awakening of Faith*, it is likewise taught that the untainted dharmas possess three types of perfuming, as will be seen below. Question:

According to the tenet of this treatise, do all sentient beings inherently possess the untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) by their very nature (*dharmatā*)? Answer: From beginningless time, they are inherent by their very nature.
One who possesses the innate, untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) of a bodhisattva is called one of the bodhisattva lineage;

one who possesses the three kinds of innate, untainted seeds is called one of indeterminate lineage; one who possesses the innate, untainted seeds of a pratyekabuddha is called one of the fixed pratyekabuddha lineage;
and one who possesses the innate, untainted seeds of a śrāvaka is called one of the fixed śrāvaka lineage. There is no [lineage] devoid of the three vehicles.
By the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), those who lack the untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) are called "beings without nature" (*agotra*).
Because they will cycle through birth and death until the end of the future, never attaining the state of a noble one of the three vehicles, they are named "those without nature.

Those of the two vehicles with fixed natures enter the remainderless nirvana (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), where the body is extinguished and wisdom ceases, becoming identical with the pure *dharmadhātu* of true thusness (*tathatā*). They do not follow the enumeration of sentient beings, nor do they follow that which is non-sentient.

Because their dispositions (*gotra*) are fixed, they are called those of "fixed nature" (*niyata-gotra*); as for those of "unfixed nature" (*aniyata-gotra*), because Buddhas and Bodhisattvas through their conditions cause them to turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle and subsequently attain the fruit of Buddhahood, they are called those of "unfixed nature.

This meaning is explained extensively; as Master Ji has cited various sacred teachings in his *Kouyao*, I fear it would be too prolix to collect them all here, so I leave it to the broad-minded and learned.
Now, based on this, I shall provide a general overview according to the school of the *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna*.

In brief, there are four types of perfuming (*vāsanā*) regarding the mutual interaction and continuous arising of defilement and purity. First is the perfuming of pure dharmas (*śukla-dharma-vāsanā*).
This refers to the intrinsically pure original enlightenment (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara-ādi-bodhi*) within the gate of arising and ceasing; this is termed a "pure dharma.

The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* and the *Gandhahastin* state that it is a pure dharma for three reasons: first, because its essence is primordially pure; second, because its characteristics involve internal perfuming.
It causes that which is subject to defilement to return to its original purity; thus, the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha) of the Liang dynasty states:
"That which establishes [the result] refers to the ten kinds of merit of True Suchness (*tathatā*), and that which is established refers to the ten kinds of newly arising correct practices.

Third, regarding the perfuming of function, it serves as the pure condition that accords with the capacities of sentient beings. Second, regarding the perfuming of fundamental ignorance, it is what is called the cause of all defiled phenomena.
First, the six defilements and the nine characteristics all arise because the ocean of the single mind is stirred by the perfuming of ignorance;

therefore, they all exist because of ignorance. Second, the perfuming of the beginningless deluded mind refers to what are called the *karmic consciousness* (*ālayavijñāna*) and the *discriminating consciousness of phenomena*;
if one traces them to their source, they are simply the *karmic consciousness*. Fourth, the perfuming of delusive objects.

What is practiced are the so-called six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), which are the spheres of the *vastu-vijñāna* (the consciousness of things). Therefore, while the pure dharmas are spoken of as one, the defiled dharmas are spoken of as three.

The Venerable Gandhahastin said: "Because these defiled dharmas possess distinctions in their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) based upon causes and conditions, they are fully explained as being of three types.
Although the pure dharmas are established in meaning in contrast to the defiled, their essence and function remain ultimately undifferentiated; therefore, [they are not further divided].
To clarify one point for the sake of elucidating the various meanings discussed above, the treatise states:
"Furthermore, because there are four kinds of dharmas that function through perfuming (*vāsanā*), the arising of defiled and pure dharmas continues without interruption. What are these four?

First, the pure dharma is called *tathatā* (Suchness)—[the *Tāishì* and *Xiànglóng* commentaries both state this refers to *tathatā* within the gate of arising-and-ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-dvāra*), and not the gate of Suchness itself, because the latter lacks the principle of perfuming and arising]. Second, all causes of defilement are called..."

The three deluded minds are called the *karmic consciousness* (the *xiang* commentary states that this also encompasses the *consciousness of phenomena* and the *ālaya-karmic consciousness*; here, however, it refers only to the "karmic consciousness" because it is based on their root).
Fourth is the deluded objective realm, namely the six sense-objects (*ṣad-viṣaya*). (The above is a brief citation of the name "perfuming"; as for the meaning of perfuming:
it is like clothing in the world which originally has no fragrance, yet if a person perfumes it with incense, it then possesses a fragrant scent. (The above explains the term "perfuming.")
This is also like that: True Suchness (*tathatā*) is a pure dharma and is truly without defilement; however, because it is perfumed by ignorance (*avidyā*), the appearance of defilement arises.

The *Xiangxiang shi* (Fragrant Elephant Commentary) explains: "Because of perfuming, there is the appearance of defilement" means this reveals that while True Suchness is signless (*animitta*), it manifests according to perfuming;
furthermore, it reveals that false dharmas have no substantial essence, which is why they are merely called "appearances," and these appearances themselves lack inherent existence.

Because it refers to the function of returning [to the source], it speaks of "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) and not "function" (*vṛtti*). This is explained according to the Gate of Arising and Ceasing that follows the flow.
This interpretation of the Tathāgatagarbha within the sūtra—stating that it is perfumed by beginningless evil habits and undergoes arising and ceasing—is as the *Awakening of Faith* says:

"The defiled dharmas of ignorance are in reality devoid of pure karma; yet, because they are perfumed by True Suchness (*tathatā*), there exists the function of purity. (As cited in the *Xiangxiang*).

The commentary states: This refers to the principle of permeation (*vāsanā*) existing within the True Suchness of Original Enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*) in the Gate of Arising and Ceasing; however, this principle does not exist within the Gate of True Suchness itself.

Because this internal permeation of Original Enlightenment causes non-enlightenment to give rise to weariness [with suffering] and a longing [for liberation], thereby turning in accord with the True [Suchness], it is called "function.
This explains the passage in the Sūtra stating that because of the existence of the *tathāgatagarbha*, one is able to weary of the suffering of birth and death and joyfully seek *nirvāṇa*.
The *Panya-nirvāṇa-sūtra* states that those who are icchantikas will, by the power of their future Buddha-nature, give rise once again to roots of goodness.
What is called "the power of Buddha-nature" is precisely the power of this intrinsically perfuming original enlightenment (*prakṛti-awakening*).

Based on this passage, the tenet of this treatise asserts that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature and shall all attain the fruit of Buddhahood; such is the case regarding the five natures (*pañca-gotra*) and so forth.

Regarding these, they are explained in detail according to the gate of habitual nature (*śīla-gotra*) and the gate of the supporting basis (*āśraya*), as seen in the *Gandhahastin-śāstra-vibhāga* and Kuei-chung’s *Ten Gates on the Harmonization of Disputes*.
Generally speaking, the meaning of perfuming (*vāsanā*) has two types:
first, "perfuming through habituation," which refers to the perfuming of the substance of the mind (*citta-svabhāva*) to bring about defilement, purity, and so forth.
Second, the mutual support of perfuming refers to the interaction between the manifest mind and its objects, as well as the various afflictions.
However, in order to clarify the general meaning of this perfuming, one first clarifies the perfuming of defiled dharmas, followed by the perfuming of pure dharmas.
Regarding the meaning of the perfuming of defiled dharmas, there are briefly six points explained from shallow to deep: first, false objects.

The meaning of "perfuming" (*vāsanā*) has two aspects: first, the perfuming that increases the power of mindfulness, which refers to the continuity of conceptual thoughts of dharmic attachment—the marks of cognition—within the *pravṛtti-vijñāna* (empirical consciousness), arising through the power of objects;

second, the perfuming that increases grasping, which refers to the marks of clinging and the marks of calculating names within the *pravṛtti-vijñāna*, namely the afflictions of self-view, craving, and delusion.
By these two meanings, it is clarified that the deluded mind is stirred by the influence of objective realms. Second, regarding the meaning of the deluded mind’s perfuming, there are also two kinds.
First is the fundamental perfuming of the *ālayavijñāna* (karmic consciousness). The *Xiangxiang* (Fragrant Elephant) Commentary states:

"This means that the karmic consciousness is able to provide the support for the perfuming of the ignorance residing in the ground (*mūlavidyā*), which, being deluded regarding the signless, can give rise to the evolving aspect (*pravṛtti-lakṣaṇa*) and the manifesting aspect (*nimitta-lakṣaṇa*), causing them to continue in succession."

Although those of the three vehicles have transcended the triple world and, despite their reliance on the consciousness of fragmented existence (*vibhava-vijñāna*), still undergo the gross suffering of birth and death, they nevertheless endure the subtle suffering of the *ālaya-vijñāna*’s transformative flux (*pariṇāma-saṃskāra-duḥkha*).

While this subtle suffering does not exist for the Tathāgata, it is spoken of here because, at the stage where one has already abandoned gross suffering and its characteristics become manifest, one must distinguish the subtle from the gross.
As the treatise says: "The fundamental perfuming of the single karmic consciousness is capable of undergoing [the state of] an Arhat..."

Because the Pratyekabuddhas of the Han [tradition], all Bodhisattvas, and those of the two vehicles who have attained the nature of fixedness (*niyata-gotra*) enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* due to the suffering of birth and death, this treatise maintains that they also possess three kinds of "remainder":
namely, the remainder of afflictions (*kleśa-śeṣa*), the remainder of karma (*karma-śeṣa*), and the remainder of karmic fruition (*vipāka-śeṣa*).
These remainders never cease; their bodies and minds must necessarily pass through eighty thousand kalpas before they can subsequently resolve to generate the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
Because one must necessarily attain the fruit of Buddhahood, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, in the "Chapter on the Tathāgata-nature," states:

"The dwelling places of those of the Two Vehicles—after eighty thousand, sixty thousand, forty thousand, or ten thousand kalpas—are called 'nirvāṇa'; the place where the Unsurpassed Dharma King dwells is called 'Mahāparinirvāṇa'.

According to this, although one enters that state of no-remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*) and ceases the manifest consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*), the ālayavijñāna and its conceptualizations of phenomena still persist.
Because the consciousness (*vijñāna*) perceives the suffering induced by its heavy [karmic] conditions, it naturally possesses the *ālayavijñāna* as the consciousness of karmic suffering;

furthermore, because it experiences the subtle suffering induced by the fundamental perfuming of the consciousness of karma, it is fully described in other passages as having two types of increase. Regarding the perfuming of the discriminative consciousness of phenomena (*viṣayavijñaptivijñāna*), the *Xiangxiang lun* (Treatise on the Elephant and the Incense) says:

"By means of this consciousness of phenomena, it can support and nourish the perfuming so that when [the seeds] arise, ignorance gives rise to the coarse delusions of views and craving, which are then activated."

Because one performs various karmas through body and speech, one undergoes the suffering of the segmented birth-and-death (*paricchinna-vedanā*) of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). Therefore, the Treatise says:

"Second, the habituation of the *vibhava-vijñāna* (discriminating consciousness of phenomena) increases [karmic seeds], whereby one is able to undergo the suffering bound by the karma of ordinary beings.

Third, the habituation of ignorance (*avidyā*) also has two meanings. First, regarding fundamental habituation, the *Gandhahastin* states: "Fundamental non-enlightenment (*mūla-abodha*) habituates and vibrates True Suchness (*tathatā*), thereby bringing it into manifestation."

Among the various consciousnesses such as *karma-vijñāna* (karmic consciousness) and so forth, only the first is mentioned here; therefore, the treatise refers to it as "karmic consciousness" (*karma-vijñāna*).

Herein, one may explain in detail the four characteristics of the Mahāyāna secret [teachings], all of which can be seen in the *Qixin lun ji* (Commentary on the Awakening of Faith) by the Two Virtuous Masters.

Thus, the treatise states: "The first is fundamental perfuming (*mūla-vāsanā*), because it has the sense of being able to bring about the karmic consciousness. (This refers to "the sense of karmic consciousness" simply because the first was cited for the moment; in reality, it also pertains to the evolving consciousnesses and the manifesting consciousness.)
The perfuming of views and craving arising from these two refers to the perfuming of non-awakening regarding the branches and their extremities;
it causes the substance of the mind to become the discerning consciousness (*vijñapti-vijñāna*) of phenomena. Since the extremities arise from the root, they are said to be "arising.

The *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra* states that the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*) can give rise to all afflictions of the grounds. Furthermore, another sutra states that the power of ignorance is greatest, as it is capable of moving the One [Mind].

Question: Regarding the statement that the *dharmadhātu* pervades both types of *saṃsāra*, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* and the *Awakening of Faith* speak of the "karmic consciousness" (*karmavijñāna*) and so forth, which is the *ālayavijñāna*.

Since there is the perfuming of the fundamental consciousness of karma, why do various sūtras such as the *Saṃdhinirmocana* and treatises such as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* state that the *ālayavijñāna* is "unobscured-neutral" (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), and thus, while it is that which is perfumed, it is not that which perfumes?

Regarding the meaning of "non-awakening" within the *ālaya-vijñāna* perfumed by this treatise—namely, fundamental non-awakening (*mūla-avidyā*) and derivative non-awakening (*śākhā-pratyaṅga-avidyā*)—since these are associated with ignorance (*avidyā*), they too might not be objects of perfuming (*bhāvya*).

If one were to grant this, it would contradict various sūtras and śāstras, because the *ālaya-vijñāna* possesses the four characteristics of being an object of perfuming and thus serves as that which is perfumed. [The opponent] asks: Why?
Longhui said: "In this consciousness, the mental factor of perception (*saṃjñā*) is primary; by grasping at signs and making conceptual distinctions, one fails to realize signless *tathatā*.

Therefore, it is called 'attachment to phenomena' (*dharmagrāha*) and is also termed 'ignorance' (*avidyā*). Because it does not involve the investigative deliberation that conceives of things as truly existent, it lacks other mental factors such as wisdom (*prajñā*).
Furthermore, this deluded thought is initially extremely subtle and is associated only with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom."
Because it is contrary to the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*), it does not obstruct the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).
For this reason, it is also able to receive [objects], because it is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). It is not "marked" by being extremely fragrant or foul-smelling;

rather, it is like a person’s clothing, which a seer might perceive as having a smell yet still be able to receive both fragrance and stench, for it is not extremely foul. This consciousness is likewise. As the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* says: "There is no..."
Because a reporter cannot report the meaning of extreme fragrance or stench, this section relies on the principle of magnitude and minuteness;

thus, the ālayavijñāna also possesses the universal dharma of grasping (*grāha*), which contradicts the nature of the single mind, as it is termed "discrimination" (*vikalpa*) and acts as a perfuming agent (*vāsana*).

Because the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and other treatises rely on the principle of coarse characteristics, the ālayavijñāna is non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) and is without grasping (*nirgrāha*).

Since the obstructions (*āvaraṇa*) are also merely that which is perfumed (*vāsya*), and since the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, and other scriptures establish the skill in the secrets of mind, mentation, and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*), how could one take these "secrets" literally? Question:
If that is so, why do the various treatises state that the *ālayavijñāna* is "unobscured-neutral" (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) because it lacks the obstruction of grasping (*grāha-āvaraṇa*)? If...
Regarding the statement that "those with false conceptualization (vikalpa) are unwholesome and may also be associated with delusion (moha)":
this is because there is no separate *avidyā* (ignorance) [to be associated], and because there is no association with mental factors such as wisdom (*prajñā*). It is not said to be unwholesome;

rather, it is associated only with the five universal (*sarvatraga*) mental factors and has no association with other mental factors. This point should also be considered according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
Regarding the meaning of "perfuming" (*vāsanā*), if one takes only the *ālayavijñāna* as the object perfumed (*bhāvyamāna*), this excludes such things as the eternal nature of *tathatā*.

If one takes the seven evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*)—along with their three natures of seeing and seen—as the perfuming agents (*bhāvaka*), this excludes such things as the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nature of maturation (*vipāka*).

Now, in this *Awakening of Faith*, based on the meaning of inconceivable perfuming, it is held that *tathatā* itself serves both as the object perfumed and as the perfuming agent. This is because it functions as the basis for the perfuming of karma.

The *ālayavijñāna*, such as consciousness (*vijñāna*), is both the perfumer (*vāsaka*) and the perfumed (*vāsya*). Among the six meanings of the perfuming of defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*), they function as mutual perfumers and perfumed with respect to one another;
furthermore, this can be analyzed extensively in terms of the meaning of "perfuming-movement" (*kṣobha*) and the meaning of "perfuming-production" (*janman*).
Thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* states: "Inconceivable perfuming and inconceivable transformation are the causes of the manifesting consciousness (*ādarśa-vijñāna*)."

"Grasping at various objects and the perfuming of beginningless false conceptualization are the causes of the *vikaṭa-vastu-vijñāna* (the consciousness of discriminating phenomena)," and so forth, as explained at length.

Regarding this, Xiangxiang (Fragrant Elephant) explains: "Inconceivable perfuming" means that while ignorance can perfume True Suchness (*tathatā*), it cannot perfume that which is not subject to perfuming;
nevertheless, because it does perfume, it is called "inconceivable perfuming. Furthermore, perfuming is itself non-perfuming; this perfuming of non-perfuming is what is meant by the name.

"Unconceivable perfuming and unconceivable transformation" means that the *tathatā*-mind, while being incapable of undergoing change when perfumed by ignorance, is nevertheless able to undergo transformation;
thus it is called "unconceivable transformation. Furthermore, this transformation is itself non-change, and the transformation of that which is non-changing is termed "unconceivable transformation.
Regarding its being the cause of the *ādarśa-vijñāna* (the mirror-consciousness), within this there is also the evolving *karma-vijñāna*; the coarse is mentioned to include the subtle.
Therefore, it is called the "manifesting consciousness" (*khyāti-vijñāna*) because it grasps various objects;

that is to say, the various realms manifested by this manifesting consciousness can, in turn, stir that ocean of mind to give rise to the waves of the various functioning consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).

Regarding "the perfuming of beginningless false conceptualization": within that ocean of the combined mind, the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of deluded thoughts have been perfumed continuously since time immemorial. This...

Because the dust-like objects and mental conceptions perfuming and stirring the ocean of the mind give rise to various consciousnesses, they are called the "discriminating consciousness of phenomena" (*vāsanā-prativikalpa-vijñāna*);

this refers to its causes and so forth. Second, to clarify the perfuming of pure dharmas: the *Xiangxiang* (Fragrant Elephant) commentary states that, generally speaking, there are briefly two meanings.
First, True Suchness internally perfumes ignorance, causing it to become pure karma; this is the fundamental perfuming (*mūla-vāsanā*). Second, this pure function returns [to the source].
To infuse True Suchness (tathatā) so as to increase its power is what is meant by "new infusion" (*navasaṃskāra*). Regarding this meaning, the treatise asks:

"How does the perfuming that gives rise to pure dharmas proceed without interruption? It is said: "By means of the dharma of True Suchness, it is able to perfume ignorance (this is 'original perfuming,' *mūlasaṃskāra*);
by the power of the causes and conditions of this perfuming, it causes the deluded mind to loathe the suffering and pleasure of saṃsāra and to seek nirvāṇa (this is 'new perfuming')."

The compiler notes that the intent of this treatise is as follows: the meaning of the true suchness (*tathatā*) of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya*), internally perfuming ignorance (*avidyā*) to secretly give rise to pure function, is termed "original perfuming" (*prakṛti-paribhāvita*).

The pure function thus arisen further perfumes the essence of original enlightenment, causing it to further give rise to the fruit produced by cultivation; this is termed "new perfuming" (*navaparibhāvita*). Regarding this new perfuming within the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*...
