The process of perfuming (*vāsanā*) is further divided into two meanings: the "natural" (*dharmatā*) and the "newly perfumed" (*navavāsanā*). This refers to the pure functioning (*vyāpāra*) arising from True Suchness (*tathatā*).

The "newly perfumed" aspect proceeds from the beginningless natural state through a continuous succession of mutual support and perfuming without interruption; this is termed the "natural seed" (*dharmatā-bīja*).

Since the fundamental awakening (*mūla-ajñāna*) of True Suchness is beginningless, its pure functioning is likewise beginningless. This pure functioning gradually increases until the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*) is attained.

Having realized the nature of the one mind, one gives rise again to pure virtues; these pure functions further perfume the seeds—this is the meaning attained by the masters of the *Dharmapāla-śāstra*.

Although the pure functions arising from True Suchness (tathatā) are beginningless, when considering function in relation to essence, the essence is innately present while the function is newly perfumed.
This newly perfumed pure function serves as the direct cause and condition [for the manifestation of Buddhahood].
The fruit of the arising of initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) is attained through the principle of obtaining the fruit by means of cultivating the cause;

because this principle is without deviation, this very purity (*viśuddhi*), although it is divided into the meanings of "newly perfumed" (*navābhyasta*) and "intrinsic" (*dharmatā*) from the perspective of its function, is designated merely as "newly perfumed" when viewed in relation to the essence of the internal perfuming of original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*), for it is produced solely through new cultivation. This is the position of the master Nanda, and he has correctly grasped this principle.

However, this pure activity serves as the direct cause for the production of the fruit; yet, if its *tathatā* (suchness) were devoid of internal perfuming (*antara-vāsana*), it could not give rise to that pure activity.
This pure activity necessarily arises from the internal perfuming of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*).

Since activity cannot exist in the absence of its substance, that which produces the fruit must necessarily arise from the perfuming of the nature of original enlightenment; therefore, it is solely the fundamental nature. (Huiyuan)
The Master Candrakīrti’s position may be understood through this approach. For this reason, the Venerable Sthiramati stated:

"If one relies on the gate of receiving a fruit based on a producing cause, the newly perfumed seeds are precisely the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), because they possess the efficacy for the production of their own fruit.
As for that original nature (*prakṛti*), it is merely the capacity of the fruit-dharma to arise; it does not [itself] possess the efficacy for the production of the fruit."
There are capacities that are designated only as "fruition-nature" (phalatva) and not as "function" (vṛtti);

therefore, according to this approach, there are only newly formed seeds and no innate seeds (prakṛtistha-bīja). This approach reflects the intention of the proponents of new perfuming (navavāsanāvādin).
According to the approach of producing fruition from nature, only the innate realm (prakṛtistha-dhātu) constitutes the seed, because it is the very self-nature (svabhāva) of the resultant phenomena.

Therefore, because newly perfumed [seeds] do not constitute the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a fruit-producing dharma, from this perspective, those new perfumings can only activate the original seeds;
they cannot themselves become the seeds that constitute the essence. This point is understood through the gate of "only originally existing seeds.
If one considers the gate of "producing fruits through conjunction," the newly perfumed seeds possess only functional capacity.
If there were no nature (svabhāva), the fruit would not arise; yet the fruit arises precisely because of its nature, and that nature itself serves as the cause.

Although the original nature exists, if there is no new perfuming (navavāsanā), there is no functional capacity. Since the production of the fruit depends on this capacity, is it not the case that this is the seed?
Therefore, according to this principle, it should be said: two kinds of seeds together produce a single fruit. This newly perfumed [seed] and the original nature stand side by side as one.
It is because the Master [Wonhyo] grasped the intent of this gate that he synthesized the tenets of all schools in the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith* as its ultimate purpose.
If one adheres dogmatically to the literal words, there is nothing that would not be rejected; if one grasps the intended meaning of the teaching, there is nothing that would not be affirmed.

The subtle art of the "One Mind and Two Gates" is verified herein. However, if we discuss this pure dharma-dharmatā-āśraya-parāvṛtti separately from the perspective of perfuming (*vāsanā*), it is as follows:

There are two kinds of perfuming (*vāsanā*), and each of these two kinds of perfuming has two meanings. Regarding the "two kinds of perfuming": first is the meaning of the perfuming of the deluded mind;
second is the meaning of the perfuming of *tathatā* (suchness). Regarding the two meanings of the perfuming of the deluded mind:

first is the perfuming of the discerning consciousness (*vijñapti-vijñāna*); second is the perfuming of the manas (*manas*). Regarding the two meanings of the perfuming of *tathatā*: first is its own essence...

Regarding the two types of mutual perfuming (*vāsanā*), first is perfuming by function. Within perfuming by the deluded mind, there is perfuming by the *vijñapti-matratā-vijñāna* (consciousness of discerning phenomena).

The Treatise states: "Because ordinary beings, followers of the Two Vehicles, and others, loathing the suffering of birth and death, proceed gradually toward the Unsurpassed Way according to their respective capacities.
The *Xiangxiang* commentary states: "The consciousness of discerning phenomena is precisely the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). This is because...
Because consciousness does not know that the various objects are merely consciousness, it clings to the notion that there are truly existent external realms outside the mind.

Although ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles may give rise to the aspiration for liberation, they still regard saṃsāra as something to be loathed and nirvāṇa as something to be delighted in;
failing to understand the principle of "mind-only," they subsequently, through the power of such mental attention, eventually attain bodhi after a long period of time.

Regarding the statement that "the perfuming of the consciousness that discriminates phenomena (*vicitra-vijñapti*) leads gradually toward the Unsurpassed Way," it is called the "perfuming of the mind" (*manas*) when speaking from the perspective of its fundamental nature;

however, when discussed in general terms, it refers to the five kinds of *manas*. (These are the *ālaya*, the three [sensory] consciousnesses, the *jñeya-āvaraṇa-vijñāna*, and the *prabandha-vijñāna*—these constitute the five kinds of *manas*).
Because the Bodhisattvas realize that all phenomena are merely the measure of consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*), they abandon that consciousness which discriminates phenomena.

Since the external calculations and discriminations have already been understood as being merely mind, the progression toward the principle is swift, differing from the gradual awakening mentioned previously;

therefore, the treatise speaks of two types of mental cultivation (*manasikāra*). "Cultivation by the mind" refers to the Bodhisattva’s courageous aspiration, which leads swiftly toward *nirvāṇa*. Question:

Since the deluded mind herein is simultaneously cultivated within True Suchness (*tathatā*) and gives rise to the flow of returning [to its source], and since this cultivation by the mind belongs to the *ālayavijñāna*, how can it act independently?

Regarding the practice undertaken after generating the resolve for enlightenment: it is answered that ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles do not awaken to the *ālayavijñāna*, but instead generate the resolve and engage in practice by relying on the sustaining power of the *pravṛttivijñāna* (the consciousness of differentiated phenomena). Because this does not contradict their original nature, they are directed toward Great Bodhi;

however, as this path is indirect and remote, it is called "gradual. Once these bodhisattvas have realized the *ālayavijñāna* as the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), they then rely upon this very consciousness for their sustenance.
Only through power can one resolve to practice in order to realize the fundamental source; because this leads toward great Bodhi, being both intimate and proximate, it is called "swift.
This is distinguished according to the mutual support of the basis (*āśraya*), clarifying that it is not a matter of each [factor] generating the mind independently.

The meaning revealed here is that the pure function of the bodhicitta arises from the internal permeation of original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*); this is that which was previously obscured by the arising of ignorance.
The mind does not arise from pure karma; rather, it is merely by way of the stages of this consciousness that perfuming (*vāsanā*) is distinguished.

In reality, however, it arises from the fundamentally awakened mind (*prakṛti-āśraya*). Therefore, it is said that perfuming and so forth are distinguished by means of the mutual support of their respective bases.

Regarding the perfuming of True Suchness (*tathatā-vāsanā*), as for the perfuming of its own essential nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa-vāsanā*), the Treatise says: "From time immemorial, it has been endowed with untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) and fully equipped [with them]."

There is the nature of the objective realm created by inconceivable karma; based on these two meanings, they are constantly perfumed and, because they possess power, they enable sentient beings to weary of the suffering of birth and death, to joyfully seek nirvana, and to gain self-confidence that their own bodies possess the *tathatā* (suchness) dharma, thereby giving rise to the aspiration for enlightenment and practicing cultivation.
Xiangxiang’s commentary states: "The fundamental awakening of non-emptiness is called the untainted (*anāsrava*) dharma; this dharma..."
Because this subtle permeation (*míng xūn*) of sentient beings cannot be understood by ordinary objects, it is called "inconceivable activity" (*bùsīyì yè*).

Here, "activity" refers to the function of this subtle permeation. Regarding its "forming the nature of the objective realm," this clarifies that it does not merely permeate that deluded mind to cause it to develop weary detachment and become the observing wisdom;
rather, it also serves as the observed object for that observing wisdom. By means of these two—[the observing wisdom and the observed object]—...

The phrase "the Dharma and so forth" reveals the function of perfuming; that is to say, these two meanings—object and mind—or these two dharmas of essence and characteristic, mutually perfume sentient beings because they possess power, thereby causing them to give rise to practices such as revulsion and seeking.

The phrase "self-confidence and so forth" clarifies the manner in which cultivation arises based on perfuming. Regarding the "function-perfuming" within the perfuming of *tathatā*, the treatise states:

That which functions as perfuming (*vāsanā*) is the power of external conditions for sentient beings. Such external conditions have immeasurable meanings; briefly stated, there are two kinds. What are these two?
First, the differentiated condition (*viśeṣa-pratyaya*); second, the equalizing condition (*samatā-pratyaya*). The Equal-Fragrance Elephant explains:
"The differentiated condition acts as a condition for the perfuming of the *vastu-vijñāna* (object-consciousness) in ordinary beings and others; that is to say, it manifests..."
Because their forms are not identical, they are said to be "distinctive" (*viśeṣa*); it may also be because they serve as conditions for sentient beings with distinctive capacities.
This means that those from the three stages of worthiness (*tri-śaikṣa*) up to all Buddhas can act as such conditions.

As for what is called "equal conditions" (*samatā-pratyaya*), it refers to acting as a condition for the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*) and its habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of all Bodhisattvas; because only the manifestation of the Buddha-body is equal and non-dual, it is called "equal."

It may also serve as a condition for the mechanism of the impartial mind (*samacitta*). This means that from the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) upward, up to all Buddhas, one must rely on the power of the wisdom of identical essence (*tongti zhibili*); because this [power] can act as a support, it serves as this condition. As the Treatise says:
"Regarding the impartial condition, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas universally vow to deliver all sentient beings; through natural permeation (*vāsanā*), they never cease [this effort]."
By means of the power of the wisdom of the identity of essence, one asks: for what reason are these two conditions called the "True Suchness (Tathatā) perfuming through its activity"?
The answer is: because Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and so forth are all manifested from my own One Mind, and there is no other separate dharma;

this is the meaning of the "Great Activity" of the True Suchness of Original Enlightenment. Therefore, the *Mahāvaipulya-maṇi-alaṃkāra-sūtra* says: "One sees for oneself one's own body as the fruit of the future."
The Buddha rubs [the disciple’s] head and preaches the Dharma; the distinct activities of body and mind are inconceivable.

Furthermore, this treatise states that because one does not know that the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) are manifesting, one perceives [objects] as coming from the outside and grasps at the boundaries of form and so forth.

My single-minded fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*), when permeated by cultivation, becomes the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and so on. Question: If these two types of permeation—defiled and pure—are ever exhausted?
Question: Is there also no exhaustion [of the pure]? Answer: The Elephant of Fragrance (Gandhahastin) says that defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*) oppose the Truth;

because they have a beginning but an end, when one reaches the source of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), those defiled phenomena and their perfuming (*vāsanā*) also come to an end. Pure phenomena (*vyavadāna-dharma*), however, accord with the Principle;

they have a beginning but no end. Although one has already attained Buddhahood, the arising of pure phenomena and their perfuming likewise have no end, for the inconceivable functioning of manifesting transformations (*nirmāṇa*) continues without cessation.

Because they are completely exhausted, the Treatise explains the meaning of this exhaustion and non-exhaustion as follows: "Furthermore, defiled dharmas have been perfuming [the mind] uninterruptedly since beginningless time;
even until the attainment of Buddhahood, they are subsequently severed. Pure dharmas, however, have no severance or exhaustion in the future.
Why is this so? Because the Dharma of True Suchness (tathatā) constantly perfumes [the mind], the deluded mind is thereby extinguished."
Because the Dharmakāya manifests and gives rise to activity through the perfuming of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), there is no interruption. Question:

Since one has already attained the fruit of Buddhahood and exhausted the source of the mind, why is it that the perfuming of pure dharmas never ceases or comes to an end? Is it not the case that there may be degrees of superiority or inferiority in the virtues of Buddhas across different times, given that earlier Buddhas have undergone perfuming for a longer duration?
Answer: In the school of Vijñaptimātra, although the principle of the Dharmakāya is of a single flavor, the wisdom-Dharmakāya...
The distinctions between the preceding and succeeding Buddhas are like the light of a lamp: though they appear in successive layers, they do not obstruct one another;
though they pervade all, they are neither disordered nor separate. Thus, the Buddhas of the past and future in this *Awakening of Faith* are all but the One Mind, possessing no other essence.

It is only due to the discrimination of deluded thoughts that each is termed "self" or "other. If delusion is stilled and the truth is discussed, there is no difference between the former and the latter.

Since the Buddha of initial awakening (shijue) is identical to original awakening (benjue) and lacks any distinction of "initial" versus "original," there is no fault of temporal sequence or hierarchical superiority.
Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Sentient beings falsely discriminate, thinking 'this is the Buddha' or 'this is the world. If one understands reality, there is neither Buddha nor world.
This is because one has exhausted the true source of the single mind and reached the reality within the myriad phenomena; therefore, [these distinctions] do not exist.

How could there be a distinction in the Buddha-body when the Buddha-realm is itself unique? Furthermore, the *Treatise* states: "Initial awakening (śikṣābodha) is identical to fundamental awakening (mūlabodha).
Since one has reached the source of the Dharma-realm, where there is no difference between delusion and enlightenment, how could there be a distinction between the fundamental and the initial?
Therefore, it is said that they are "identical to fundamental awakening. Question: Does this *Awakening of Faith* treatise contain the seeds for both defiled and pure perfuming?
Question: Regarding the six meanings [of a cause], the answer is that according to the *Gandhahastin*’s explanation of the *Pratītyasamutpāda*, even a seed can possess all six meanings.

Thus, the middle fascicle of the *Jiaoshen fenzhi lun* (Treatise on the Classification of the Profound Meaning of the Teachings) asks: "If that is so, since a present action serves as the causal seed, how can it possess the six meanings? The answer is:

they do not possess them in their entirety according to what is predominant, as explained in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and other texts. That seeds possess six meanings refers to the initial teaching of the Mahāyāna; if one were to consider...
The profound meaning of dependent origination in the Final Teaching (Zhōngjiào) fully possesses these six meanings.

This is because, within this teaching, the sixth and seventh consciousnesses (*ṣaṣṭha-vijñāna* and *saptama-vijñāna*) are also the Tathāgatagarbha following conditions, having no separate self-nature; thus, the seventh consciousness also possesses the six meanings found within the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*).

Reflect upon this. A detailed explanation of the six meanings is provided in the chapter on the "Six Causes" (*ṣaḍ-hetu*); as it would be too prolix, it is not included here. Question: Only... [text ends]

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only) posits that "intrinsic seeds" (*dharmatā-bīja*) refer to the nature of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), whereas this treatise [the *Ratnagotravibhāga*] posits that "intrinsic nature" (*dharmatā*) refers to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
What authoritative scripture serves as the mirror for this? Answer: The *Ratnagotravibhāga* states:
"The nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is as explained in the *Ṣaḍāyatanasamudgama-sūtra*: 'From beginningless time, it has been the ultimate consummation of all phenomena.'"

Because it is the essence, the *Anuttarāśraya-sūtra* also contains this passage; this serves as proof by clarifying the meaning of the beginningless, natural order (*dharmatā*) with respect to the unconditioned nature (*asaṃskṛta-dhātu*).
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "The excellence of the six perfections has such characteristics:

they have been transmitted from one to another since beginningless time and are obtained through the natural order. This clarifies the beginningless [nature] with respect to the conditioned nature (*saṃskṛta-dhātu*).
Because this is the fundamental principle from the outset, one should understand through this text that the tenets of the two treatises differ.
Regarding the sixth section, the "Gate of Establishing the Similarities and Differences of the Three Bodies":

in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and the four categories of wisdom-mind (*catur-jñāna-citta-varga*) together constitute the five dharmas, which are named the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Within this Dharma-body, the three bodies are separately distinguished.
The pure dharma-realm constitutes the svabhāvakāya; when combined with the self-enjoyment and other-enjoyment [bodies], it is called the sambhogakāya;
and when established in conjunction with the pure and impure realms, it is named the nirmāṇakāya, also called the *nirmāṇa-kāya*. Thus, the tenth fascicle of the treatise states:

"These two fruits attained by the Muni are forever free from the two obstacles and are also called the dharmakāya, possessing immeasurable and boundless great merits such as the powers (*bala*) and fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*)."
Because it is adorned by the dharmas, the collection of their essential natures is collectively termed "body" (*kāya*). This *dharmakāya* has five factors as its nature;
it is not the pure *dharmadhātu* alone that is called the *dharmakāya*, for both results of the two-fold transformation (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) are subsumed within it.

Thus, this *dharmakāya* has three distinct aspects: first, the *svabhāvakāya* (Essential Body), which refers to the true, pure *dharmadhātu* of all Tathāgatas, [and the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*].
The basis of the equality of transformation is quiescent, free from signs, and transcends all conceptual proliferation; it possesses infinite, true, and eternal qualities.
This is the equal, ultimate nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*). This very self-nature is also called the *dharmakāya*, for it is the support for the dharmas of great merit.
Second, there are two kinds of *saṃbhogakāya*: first, the *svasaṃbhogakāya*, which refers to the [bodies] of all Tathāgatas...
The *svasaṃbhogakāya* (body of self-enjoyment) arises from the cultivation and accumulation of immeasurable provisions of merit and wisdom over three incalculable eons;

it is characterized by boundless, true qualities and an extremely pure, eternal, and pervasive form-body that remains serene throughout the succession of time until the end of the future, constantly enjoying the vast dharma-pleasure for oneself.
The *parasaṃbhogakāya* (body of enjoyment for others) refers to those manifested by the Tathāgatas through their wisdom of equality.

The Body of Subtle and Pure Merit dwells in a purely pure land; for the assembly of bodhisattvas who abide on the ten stages, it manifests great supernormal powers, turns the wheel of the true Dharma, and resolves the nets of doubt of the multitude, causing them to enjoy the bliss of the Mahāyāna Dharma.

When these two aspects are combined, it is called the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*). Third is the Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*), which refers to the Tathāgata’s manifestation through the wisdom of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).

The *Pramāṇa* [treatises] explain that the Transformation Body (nirmāṇakāya) manifests in pure and impure lands according to its kind, appearing to bodhisattvas who have not yet reached the bhūmis, as well as to those of the two vehicles and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), manifesting supernatural powers and preaching the Dharma in accordance with their respective capacities so that each may obtain various benefits and happiness;

this is explained at length. Furthermore, the five dharmas are subsumed within the three bodies (*trikāya*); the detailed and extensive alternative explanations are exactly as stated therein, and likewise...
In Master Ji’s *Fayuan Sanshen Yi Zhang* (Chapter on the Meaning of the Three Bodies), regarding the discussion of permanence and impermanence according to the intent of the treatises:
the Dharma-body is permanent because it is the self-nature; yet it is also impermanent because of its being both separated from and not separated from [adventitious defilements].

The merit produced through cultivation is impermanent because it arises from causes; however, as it is conditioned yet untainted (*anāsrava*), it may also be considered permanent because it is uninterrupted.
Therefore, because they arise in a continuous succession, the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* states: "By nature, they continue without interruption; the three Buddhas are eternally abiding.

Now, based on this, the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* explains that the differentiated appearances of the six realms as perceived by ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles are called the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body).
That which is seen by Bodhisattvas of the ten stages and above—being free from the limitations of form—is called the *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense body), which is far removed [from such limitations].
The distinction between matter and mind, as well as the differentiation between identity and difference, are subsumed within the universal essence of all phenomena.
That which is neither conceptualizable nor cognizable, yet is unimpeded reality, is called the *dharmakāya*. As the treatise states: "Furthermore, regarding the function of *tathatā*...
even so, no characteristic of function can be apprehended. Why? Because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are bodies whose very nature is the wisdom of the *dharmakāya*."
The ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) has no realm of worldly truth (saṃvṛti-satya) and is free from conditioned activity (*abhisamskāra*)—this above clarifies the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
However, because it brings benefit according to the seeing and hearing of sentient beings, it is spoken of as "function" (*vṛtti*). This function is of two kinds. What are the two?

First, that which is seen by the minds of ordinary people and those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), relying on the consciousness of discriminating phenomena (*vikalpa-vastu-vijñāna*), is called the Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*); this is because they do not know...
First, because the evolving consciousnesses manifest, one perceives [the Buddha] as coming from outside; grasping at the boundaries of form, one is unable to know them exhaustively.

Second, based on the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*), it refers to that which is seen by a Bodhisattva from the initial arousal of the mind—[the first arousal of the mind being called the "Abode of Initial Arousal" within the ten stages of understanding]—up to the mind of the Bodhisattva’s ultimate stage.
What is seen is called the *saṃbhoga-kāya* (recompense body). This body possesses immeasurable forms, and each form possesses immeasurable [qualities].
From their marks (*lakṣaṇa*) up to whatever is manifested, they are boundless and inexhaustible;
such meritorious qualities are accomplished through the perfuming of the untainted practices of the *pāramitās* and the inconceivable perfuming.

Because they are fully endowed with the marks of immeasurable bliss, they are called "retribution" (*vipāka*). Furthermore, what is seen by ordinary beings is its coarse form (*rūpa*). Following this...
Within the six realms of existence, various distinct classes of beings are each seen differently because they do not possess the characteristics of experiencing pleasure;

therefore, it is called the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body), as explained extensively in that [text]. However, according to the intent of this treatise, regarding such matters as permanence and impermanence, Xiangxiang (*Gandhahastin*) states there are two meanings:
first, a specific explanation, and second, a general statement. Within the specific explanation, the meritorious qualities produced through cultivation are impermanent, because they are cultivated.
Because it arises, it is also eternally one; once attained, it is identical with True Suchness (*tathatā*). Why is this?
Because it originally flows from the Truth, and once ignorance has been exhausted, it returns to the essence of the Truth. As the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra) of the Liang dynasty states:
"There is nothing that does not flow from this Dharmakāya, and there is nothing that does not return to realize this Dharmakāya. It further says: "It is like empty space, which pervades all things."

The limit of form (*rūpa-paryanta*) is without arising, abiding, ceasing, or transformation; the Tathāgata’s wisdom is likewise, pervading all that is knowable, non-erroneous, and without transformation.
Therefore, one should know that it is not merely constant because it is uninterrupted, but is also eternally unchanging like True Suchness (*tathatā*).
The Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is eternal because, while conforming to conditions, its own nature remains unchanging.
This [aspect] is impermanent because it arises in accordance with defilement. Why? Because all meritorious qualities are simultaneously identical to True Suchness;

therefore, the arising of their function is exclusively the work of the True. Thus, in this *Awakening of Faith*, the two bodies—the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and the Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*)—are subsumed under the function of True Suchness.
Furthermore, it says: "When the minds of sentient beings are pure, the images of the Dharma-body appear," and so forth. It further states: "Moreover, Original Enlightenment follows..."
The two kinds of marks produced by the discrimination of defilement are inseparable from that original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya*). That is to say:
first, the mark of the purity of wisdom; second, the mark of inconceivable activity—and so on, as explained at length.

Because this Dharmakāya functions in accordance with conditions, the distinctions among its merits are thereby established; because it possesses the quality of immutability, there are no merits that are not present.

Because the two meanings—that the true nature (tathatā) follows along with all phenomena through its entire substance while its characteristics remain unchanging—are fused together without obstruction, the fruit of Buddhahood is both permanent and impermanent, possessing the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) or being beyond them; this should be understood according to the context. Question:

If that is so, why is it said that [the Buddha] is neither one nor different? Answer: Because in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, it is stated that since True Suchness (*tathatā*) is pervasive, wisdom...
Because it realizes suchness (*tathatā*), it is not different [from it]; because the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) are not identical, it is not one [with it].

Now, in this *Awakening of Faith*, there are two meanings of "virtue" (*guṇa*): first, the meaning of the manifestation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), because the merit accumulated over three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) is not in vain;
second, the meaning of the absence of self-nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), because apart from suchness, there is no essence. Of these, the former is the primary meaning here.
The latter meaning—of the *dharmakāya* following conditions—is not a different gate from the former meaning—of the *dharmakāya* being unchanging;
rather, it is the total inclusion of the whole essence. Furthermore, this initial meaning—of the *dharmakāya* being unchanging—is not the same gate as the latter meaning—of its following conditions;
for while they are not one, their meanings are distinct. Thus, by being immovable yet not different, it clarifies that they are not identical. Question: Both of these two schools...

Question: How can these conflicting points be reconciled to serve as the foundation of this treatise? Answer: The *Xiangxiang* (Fragrant Elephant) reconciles them by first relying on the Initial Teaching of the Mahāyāna and subsequently resorting to the Final Teaching of the Mahāyāna; since the teachings possess varying degrees of depth, there is no fault.

As for Master Jizang’s reconciliation of the differing explanations regarding the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the various *Śāstras*, he states that according to the *Sūtra on the Similarity of Natures*, attaining Buddhahood in an impure land is termed "transformation body" (*nirmāṇakāya*).

Attaining enlightenment in the Pure Land is called the *sambhogakāya* (Enjoyment Body). The *Suvarṇaghaṭa-sūtra* states that the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics and so forth are called the *nirmāṇakāya* (Emanation Body).
The body manifested according to the six realms of existence is called the *nirmāṇakāya*.

According to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, that which is seen prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) is called the *nirmāṇakāya*, while that which is seen from the stages onward is called the *sambhogakāya*. Thus it is.
In the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, the distinct appearances of the six realms as perceived by ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles are called the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body);
that which is perceived by Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), being free from the limitations of form, is called the *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense body).

The reason they differ in this way is that the gates of the Dharma are immeasurable and do not follow a single path; therefore, whatever is established according to circumstances possesses its own underlying principle.

The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that what is perceived by the distracted mind prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) possesses limited characteristics (*sāvadhika-lakṣaṇa*), and therefore belongs to the Nirmāṇakāya.
However, this treatise clarifies that what is perceived by the samādhi of this Bodhisattva is free from limited characteristics; therefore, it belongs to the Saṃbhogakāya.

By this reasoning, there is no contradiction. As for the "collection" (*saṃcaya*), it is said that the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī) explains it in terms of the conceivable causes of perfuming (*bhāvanā-hetu*).

Regarding the gates of the fruit and its support, it is clarified that although the Dharma-body of principle (*li-fǎshēn*) and the Dharma-body of wisdom (*zhì-fǎshēn*) are not separate, the principle is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) while wisdom is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*);

thus, there is a distinction between their essence and function. Now, in this *Awakening of Faith*, within the gate of inconceivable perfuming, cause and effect, and dependent origination, the three bodies are explained:
though they are distinct, the reward body (*sambhogakāya*) and the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) are the great functioning of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Because principle is itself wisdom and wisdom is itself principle, a sutra states: "The emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) is called wisdom," and so forth.
Because form is itself mind and mind is itself form, a treatise states: "This very Dharmakāya is the substance of form, and is thus able to manifest as form.
This is because, from the very beginning, form and mind have been non-dual; since the nature of form is itself wisdom.
Therefore, because the substance of form is formless, it is called the "wisdom-body" (*jñānakāya*); and because the nature of wisdom is itself form, it is called the "dharma-body" (*dharmakāya*).

Pervading all places, the forms manifested therein have no boundaries; according to the mind, they can manifest the infinite adornments of the worlds of the ten directions, each distinct from the other, yet all without boundary and without mutual obstruction. This is not a portion of the mind-consciousness (*citta-vijñāna*).
Because it can separately know the meaning of the sovereign function of *tathatā* (suchness), the characteristics of its meaning are explained extensively as in other places;
for now, the discussion of similarities and differences is briefly concluded here.

Regarding the seventh section, the "Establishment of the Similarities and Differences of Grasping and Obstructions," in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the grasping at a person (*pudgala-grāha*) is established as the primary root.

The afflictions (*kleśa*)—such as anger, resentment, concealment, and vexation—and the various secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) constitute the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the afflictive obstruction (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Its attendants (*parivāra*) consist of the factors associated with them, the karma they produce, and the fruits thereof, which are subsumed within the substance of the afflictive obstruction.

As for the cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), it is headed by the attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), consisting of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*) and craving for phenomena (*dharmatṛṣṇā*), along with pride (*māna*).

Taking ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth as its essence, when discussing its associated factors (*sahāya*), those mental states that are concomitant with it, as well as the objects they grasp, are also included therein.

If one analyzes the essence of the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*) based on the eight consciousnesses, it does not associate with the *ālayavijñāna*, but arises only in conjunction with the seven evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
Among these, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) are common to all seven types of consciousness, while pride (*māna*) is common to two.
It is understood that anger (*dveṣa*) does not occur in the seventh manas-consciousness; doubt (*vicikitsā*) and the four views (*dṛṣṭi*) occur only in the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Among these, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) occurs in both the mental consciousness and the manas. Within the view of a self-identity, there are two modes of activity (*ākāra*):

namely, the mode of "I" (*ahaṃkāra*) and the mode of "mine" (*mamakāra*). These two modes of activity also pertain to both consciousnesses. The meaning of these two modes is visible in the mental consciousness, while in the manas, [the mode of "I"]...

Regarding the various explanations [as follows], the Master Dharmapāla states that [the view] directly takes the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) of the ālayavijñāna as its object, conceiving it as "self" and "mine";
he says this because he follows the force of the phrasing [in the sūtras] which speaks of "mine," and so forth.

The Master Nanda and others state that [the view] takes the self-substance (svabhāva) of the ālayavijñāna as its object and forms the conception of "self," while also taking the various image-parts (nimitta-bhāga) upon the substance of that consciousness as its object and forming the conception of "mine."
The Master Daśabala-Mitra and others take the former explanation as the correct meaning, while the Master Wonhyo and others take the latter interpretation as the correct meaning.
The detailed resolution of these difficulties and reconciliation of contradictions can be seen in the "Chapter on the Two Obstructions" (*Er-zhang*).

If one analyzes the nature of the obstructions according to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), there are many gateways of the three-nature doctrine; here, however, we shall explain it based on a single gateway of self-nature (*svabhāva*), stating that form (*rūpa*) is non-existent.

All afflictions (*kleśa*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the four delusions of the *manas* in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are subsumed under the category of obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) nature.

Greed, hatred, and delusion arising from the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*) are of an unwholesome (*akuśala*) nature, as they are the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of an unwholesome mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Among those arising from the mental consciousness of the desire realm, all afflictions that arise through conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*) are entirely [unwholesome].
Among the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), the two views of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) that arise spontaneously (*svarasavāhin*) are neutral (*avyākṛta*).

Attachment, pride, and ignorance, when they give rise to unwholesome karma to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), are unwholesome (*akuśala*) in nature. At the time of linking rebirth (*pratisandhi*), their manifestation is subtle and thus neutral.
Hatred (*pratigha*) alone is exclusively unwholesome in nature. Furthermore, among the secondary afflictions, vitarka, vicāra, regret (*kaukṛtya*), and sleep (*middha*) [are as previously specified].
These four [mental factors] pervade all three natures; however, among the wholesome states, they are not necessarily of the nature of secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).

For example, when one cultivates the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) within a dream, the factor of sleep (*middha*) therein is not of the nature of a delusion (*kleśa*). The remaining three [of the four] should be understood accordingly.

The ten factors beginning with heedlessness (*pramāda*), as well as guile (*śāṭhya*), deceit (*māyā*), and arrogance (*mada*), pertain exclusively to the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the obscured-unneutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*). Wrath (*krodha*) and resentment (*upanāha*) [pertain to both].

Concealment (*mrakṣa*), vexation (*pradāśa*), avarice (*mātsarya*), envy (*īrṣyā*), harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*), lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*)—these nine types possess exclusively the nature of unwholesomeness (*akuśala*).
Regarding these, the treatise explains that lack of shame and lack of dread constitute their essential nature (*svabhāva*) and pervade all unwholesome minds.

While it is said that "dread" (*apatrāpya*) functions extensively and thus applies to all [unwholesome states], "shame" (*hrī*) does not necessarily apply to all. Nevertheless, these secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are briefly established through four aspects of differentiation.
"Established" refers to shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), which also arise in unwholesome minds;

furthermore, negligence (*pramāda*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), lethargy (*styāna*), lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), laziness (*kausīdya*), wrong desire (*mithyā-chanda*), wrong resolve (*mithyā-adhimokṣa*), wrong mindfulness (*mithyā-smṛti*), distraction (*vikṣepa*), and lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*)—these ten arise in all defiled minds.

[The following] ten—anger (*krodha*), enmity (*upanāha*), concealment (*mrakṣa*), envy (*īrṣyā*), deceit (*śāṭhya*), guile (*māyā*), arrogance (*mada*), and harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*)—each [arise in specific instances].
When a distinct unwholesome mind arises, if one [mental factor] occurs, a second necessarily does not.

Thus, these ten types are all bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), with the exception of *śāṭhya* (deceit), *māyā* (guile), and *mada* (pride). Because of *māyā* and *śāṭhya*, [these two] extend to the first *dhyāna*; *mada* extends through all three realms.

These, together with the preceding two, when in the higher stages, are exclusively of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*). Vitarka (applied thought), vicāra (sustained thought), kaukṛtya (regret), and middha (sleep)—these four—pertain to all three natures.

The mind is not present in all places or at all times; if one seeks and examines for too long, it causes the body to become exhausted and mindfulness to be lost, which is also a form of weariness and damage.
Therefore, vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought) are called secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). These two persist up to the level of the first dhyāna.
Regret (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep (*middha*) exist only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Thus, the characteristics of the afflictive hindrances have been briefly explained.

Regarding those who understand the characteristics of the obstacles, the masters of the *Dharmapāla-śāstra* and others state that the ignorance of clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha-avidyā*) exists only in the seventh and sixth consciousnesses and does not extend to the other consciousnesses, because it involves investigative seeking of their nature.

Furthermore, while attachment to phenomena, hatred, and so forth are not subsumed under "view" (*dṛṣṭi*), they do extend to the five sensory consciousnesses when they do not involve investigative seeking;
however, even these possess clinging to phenomena and do not extend to the ālayavijñāna. If there were any clinging to phenomena within this [ālaya] consciousness...
If this consciousness possessed a grasping for dharmas (dharma-grāha), it would be inconsistent with ignorance and other such factors; it would be associated only with five factors.

Furthermore, if this consciousness were to possess grasping for dharmas, there would be no basis for perfuming (vāsanā), and thus it would perish moment by moment, leading to the great error of its ceasing even without the application of an antidote.
Moreover, when the contemplation of the emptiness of dharmas first manifests, this [consciousness] should also be severed, as the obstacle and the antidote are mutually contradictory.

Because they arise simultaneously, if that were so, the remaining seeds of the outflowing (*sāsrava*) dharmas would lack a basis; the cultivated merits would lack the perfuming (*vāsanā*), as there would be nothing to be perfumed.
Furthermore, it cannot be said that the perfuming occurs in the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), because that wisdom is not indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and has not yet been attained.

Therefore, we know that the attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) does not extend to this consciousness. If [this attachment] exists only within the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), it must reside solely in the unwholesome (*akuśala*).
Although the obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) does not defile the noble paths of the two vehicles, it does obscure the path of the bodhisattvas;
for this reason, it is called both "obscured" and "unobscured," as these two names refer to different perspectives within a single entity.

It does not extend to the four types [of minds], specifically within the transformational consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna), regarding those which are the fruits of maturation (vipākaphala) and are exclusively unobscured-unspecified.
Because it is of the same nature and category as the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), its power of conceptualization is weak and it cannot grasp [objects];
because minds such as those engaged in deportment (*īryāpatha*) lack firm grasping; because it is not universal;

and furthermore, because it does not accompany all wholesome minds, being of a nature and characteristic that contradict ignorance (*avidyā*), and because it must always be associated with the wholesome root of non-delusion (*amoha*). As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi*, there are two types of ignorance.
First, there are the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and second, the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Furthermore, there are two categories: first, the defiled (*kliṣṭa*) and second, the non-defiled (*akliṣṭa*).

Since it does not mention the existence of the wholesome (*kuśala*), and so forth—if one distinguishes the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) by way of the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*), the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), the correct practice (*samyak-pratipatti*), and the five factors consisting of the mind and mental states (*citta-caitta*), the distinctions regarding the stages (*bhūmi*) and levels of severance for the treatment of these obstacles are fully detailed as in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
[Question on] the ninth and tenth consciousnesses and the gateway of practice for establishing the stages:

Among the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), which afflictions are able to project the projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*) and which produce the producing karma (*abhinirvartaka-karman*)? [Answer:

To speak generally, all afflictions project the projecting karma and also produce the producing karma. Within this context, if one selects those that are most predominant, ignorance (*avidyā*) is able to project the projecting karma.
Craving and grasping can give rise to karma. Regarding the statement that they "give rise to" (utthāpayanti) karma: they manifest and initiate projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karma*);

they give rise to productive karma (*abhinirvartaka-karma*) by causing the seeds of previously performed actions to become capable of functioning as existence (*bhava*). Thus, there are two ways in which projecting karma gives rise [to results]:
when sinful karma arises, it is given rise to by active entanglements (*paryavasthāna*); for meritorious and immovable karma, it is given rise to by latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
When projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*) arises, both demerit and merit remain unmoved, yet craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are present and capable of producing it.

Furthermore, among the projecting karmas, the co-emergent afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) produce karma for specific retribution (*vipāka-karman*), while those that arise through discrimination (*vikalpita*) produce them according to their respective conditions;
these three types can all produce the projecting karma as a whole. Question: Which afflictions are capable of linking rebirth (*pratisandhi*)? Answer: In terms of their general characteristics...

Regarding the statement that all afflictions belonging to one’s own level (*svabhūmi*) are capable of linking rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*), the most excellent [view] holds that it is solely through the innate (*sahaja*) neutral craving for self (*ātmasneha*) that the continuity of rebirth is linked.
The types of birth thus linked do not exceed two: first, actual birth (*upapattibhava*); second, birth by means (*upāyabhava*).
At the time of actual birth, there are also two kinds: those born with a material realm (*rūpadhātu*) and those born as intermediate beings (*antarābhava*).
At the time of death in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the linking of existence (*pratisaṃdhi*) occurs through the process of death-existence (*maraṇabhava*).
Regarding the mind present at the moment of death, there are three stages: first, the stage of the three wholesome natures; second, the stage of the defiled mind;
and finally, the stage of the resultant mind (*vipākacitta*). Among these, the first two belong to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), while the final single mind is the resultant mind.

Furthermore, regarding the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) within the states of mind, consciousness is not present at the moment of rebirth-linking (*pratisandhi*). Of the latter two types of mind, both belong to the stage of rebirth-linking;

moreover, between these two, the former pertains to the stage of rebirth-linking as active entanglements (*paryavasthāna*), while the latter pertains to the stage of rebirth-linking as latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).

This is explained in detail in works such as the *Yogācārabhūmi*. Question: What is the difference between the two types of grasping (*dvividha-grāha*) and the two types of hindrances (*dvividha-āvaraṇa*)? Answer: Grasping is narrow in scope, whereas hindrance is broad.
The obstacles are removed when the *ālayavijñāna* exists, yet the seven consciousnesses cling [to objects] because they are held to reside solely within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Furthermore, by clinging to the root, one obstructs the branches; for because of the internal self, external obstacles such as greed and anger arise. Question: Regarding these two obstacles, are they distinct entities or the same entity?
Answer: They are the same entity but have different functions; therefore, two names are established. Question: As for these two names based on their different functions...

What is the meaning? The answer is: The afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*) refers to delusions such as greed and anger that can induce retribution within the realms, which oppress sentient beings and cause them to depart from tranquility;
because it obstructs sentient beings from emerging from birth and death, it is called the afflictive hindrance.

The cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) refers to delusions such as the attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), which obstruct the nature of wisdom so that clear realization (*abhisamaya*) is not achieved, and veil the nature of objects.
The mind of clear realization (*abhisamaya*) is called the "obstruction to the knowable" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) for this reason:

while afflictions (*kleśa*) partially obstruct the wisdom regarding objects, they do not hinder unsurpassed enlightenment; yet even if these [afflictions] have been severed, one does not attain that [enlightenment].

Furthermore, the obstruction to the knowable partially induces cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), yet it does not obscure the nirvāṇa of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*); thus, even without severing this [obstruction], they realize it.
Because they are distinct yet share a single substance with differing functions, they are termed the "two obstacles.

Now, according to the *Awakening of Faith*, the six types of defiled mind constitute the substance of the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), while fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*) constitutes the substance of the obstacle to wisdom (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Regarding the six defilements:

first is the "defilement associated with attachment," which signifies the proliferation of the afflictions of views and craving within the mental consciousness; it consists of coarse discriminative attachment.

Because of their association, the two [types of] defilement associated with continuity are not severed; within the five kinds of manas, the consciousness of continuity arises in uninterrupted succession through its association with the grasping of dharmas—this is another name for "continuity.

The defilement associated with the threefold discriminative cognition refers to the fourth consciousness among the five kinds of manas. The defilement dissociated from the manifestation of forms refers to [the fifth consciousness] among the five kinds of manas.

The third, the manifest consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), consists of five types of defilements dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-kleśa*); these are the second type of manas within the fivefold manas.
The sixth, the fundamental karmic consciousness dissociated from mind, consists of five types of manas; this is the first, the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*) within the fivefold manas.
Among these, the first two reside in the six consciousnesses, while the third type of defilement resides in the seventh consciousness. The final three types of defilement pertain to both.
Regarding the eighth [stage], that which is called "afflictive hindrance" (*kleśāvaraṇa*) in this treatise already subsumes both obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) taught in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
Fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*) is the fundamental basis upon which those six defiled mental states depend; it is extremely subtle, dark, and non-awakened.
Internally deluded regarding its own nature—which is identical and equal—it is unable to turn outward to grasp at distinctions.

Because its characteristic is such that there is no distinction between the grasper and the grasped, and because its nature is too closely proximate to true illumination, this ignorance is most contrary to it—just as a novice śrāmaṇera is close to a senior elder (sthavira).

Among all phenomena within saṃsāra, there is not a single dharma subtler than ignorance, and its root has this alone as its source; arising suddenly at the beginning, it is therefore called by this name.
Regarding "beginningless ignorance," as the *Mūlakarma-sūtra* states: "Because no phenomena arise prior to this ground of abiding, it is called the 'ground of beginningless ignorance.
This treatise further states below: "Because one does not penetrate the single Dharma-realm, thoughts suddenly arise in a manner dissociated from the mind;
this is termed ignorance. Thus, the terms "having no prior" and "suddenly arising" do not refer to [a temporal sequence].
The temporal sequence [of the stages] is discussed here only in terms of their relative subtlety and coarseness within the process of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Thus, although this ignorance (*avidyā*) does not correspond with the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), it serves as its basis; because they are in a state of inseparable conjunction, it is only by relying upon this consciousness that its characteristics can be explained.
Consequently, it is subsumed within the state of the *ālayavijñāna*. To briefly explain the nature of these two obstructions, the treatise states: "Defiled..."
The meaning of "mind" (*citta*) is called the "obstruction of afflictions" (*kleśāvaraṇa*), because it can obstruct the fundamental wisdom of *tathatā* (suchness).

The meaning of "ignorance" (*avidyā*) is called the "obstruction of knowledge" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), because it can obstruct the spontaneous wisdom of worldly activity. The Gandhahastin’s commentary explains:

"The wondrous wisdom that illuminates stillness—the wisdom that accords with reality—is called fundamental wisdom. Because the defiled mind is agitated and noisy, it opposes this stillness; therefore, it is called 'defiled mind'."

Because they are obstructed by afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*)—due to the agitation and disturbance caused by those afflictions—one subsequently attains the wisdom of "knowing things as they are" (*yathābhūta-jñāna*), which is termed "worldly activity-wisdom" (*laukika-karma-jñāna*).
Because ignorance (*avidyā*) causes delusion and confusion such that there is no discernment, it opposes the function of this wisdom and is thus termed an "obstruction to wisdom" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

This explanation is based, for the time being, on the gate of mutual dependence between the fundamental and its derivatives: taking the defiled mind that has arisen as the obstruction of afflictions, and [taking] that which gives rise to the defiled mind...

Ignorance (*avidyā*) is defined as an obstruction to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), rather than being explained as an obstruction based on the two types of grasping—grasping at a person (*pudgala-grāha*) and grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).

Therefore, it differs from the previous school’s position. Furthermore, the two types of grasping described in this treatise also differ from those in the previous treatises. In the "Section on Counteracting Erroneous Grasping," it states:
"All erroneous graspings depend upon the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*); if one is free from the self, there is no erroneous grasping. Thus, the view of self is of two kinds.
What are the two? First, the view of a self in persons (*pudgala-ātma-dṛṣṭi*); second, the view of a self in phenomena (*dharma-ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
Regarding the view of a self in persons, it is said that there are five types based on the teachings for ordinary worldlings. What are these five?

First, having heard the Sūtras state that the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is ultimately quiescent and like empty space, because they do not understand this as being taught to destroy attachment, they immediately [mistake] it for actual empty space.

Regarding this Tathāgata-nature, up to the fifth point: because they hear the Sūtras state that "birth and death exist in dependence upon the Tathāgatagarbha" and "Nirvāṇa is attained in dependence upon the Tathāgatagarbha," yet fail to understand this, those with the view of a self (ātman) claim that sentient beings have a beginning.
Furthermore, for the sake of those of dull faculties among the two vehicles, the Tathāgata teaches only the non-existence of a personal self (pudgala-nairātmya).

Regarding the question: "It is said that there are those who do not see the ultimate truth, who fear the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), and who falsely grasp at *nirvāṇa* [while still in saṃsāra].

How can it be said that the five types of personhood-clinging (*pudgala-grāha*) explained in this treatise—which all involve conceptualizing upon the basis of True Suchness (*tathatā*)—constitute clinging to a self and persons (*ātma-pudgala-grāha*)? The Gandhahastin explains: There are two interpretations. First, it is said that these refer to beginners.
Ordinary beings who possess the notions of self and person form this attachment; therefore, it is called "attachment to self and person" (*pudgala-grāha*).

Second, because within the *tathāgatagarbha* there are two meanings: first, the meaning of original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*), which refers to the false conceptualization regarding the person, hence termed "attachment to the person";
second, the meaning of ultimate reality, which refers to the object of contemplation. Here, based on the first meaning, it is called "attachment to the person."

Question: Is the attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) so called simply because one clings to phenomena such as form and mind as being substantially real, just as one clings to them as being permanent?
Answer: Within this treatise, the two types of hindrances (*āvaraṇa*) described also possess the functional capacity to initiate karma and bind rebirth. Why is this?

Because the ground of abiding ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*) initiates uncontaminated karma (*anāsravakarma*), which enables one to undergo the transformation-death (*pariṇāmikī cyuti*) outside the realms.

This principle of the four truths without effort (*anabhisamskāra*) is as previously explained; it is the school of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*) that directly employs the gate of the four truths with effort (*sābhisamskāra*).
Therefore, in that school, a distinct cause for transformation (*pariṇāma*) is not established.

This is because the bodhisattva who attains sudden enlightenment relies upon the manifest body of a Bṛhatphala deva as an auxiliary support, whereas those who attain gradual enlightenment through the fruit [of arhatship]—specifically those of the fourth fruit who have turned their minds toward awakening [do not].
The assistance provided to the causes for manifesting a body in the desire realm serves to bring about its fruition. Regarding the first three fruits, there are two interpretations:
one states that it is like those of sudden enlightenment who have not yet severed the afflictions of the higher realms;

the other states that although they have not yet severed the afflictions of the higher realms, because they have already suppressed and detached from them, they will not undergo further rebirth, and thus the causes for manifesting a body in the desire realm are assisted so as to lead to a subtle and refined transition.
The palace of Maheśvara is established as the fruit of Buddhahood; now, based on this, the school of the *Awakening of Faith* establishes distinct causes and fruits.

Thus, among the four kinds of perfuming discussed in the treatise, it states that "the fundamental perfuming of the karmic consciousness is able to receive the three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomayakāya*) of the Three Vehicles.
This is as the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* says: "Furthermore, conditioned by the four graspings and with outflowing karma as the cause, the three [bodies] are produced."

Because there are three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*)—those of Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and powerful Bodhisattvas—which arise with the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya*) as the condition and uncontaminated karma (*anāsrava-karma*) as the cause, it is said in general that [these exist]. However, regarding the specific distinction therein, Kyūryū (Kumārajīva) explains:
"The uncontaminated karma produced herein refers to the roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*) on the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), which are not [yet] for the sake of [the ultimate fruit]."
Because that which is produced by and moistened by the three outflows (āsrava) does not undergo the three realms of existence (bhava), it is called "outflow-free" (anāsrava).

It should be known that there are two kinds of the Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya): namely, the outflowing Truth of Origination and the outflow-free Truth of Origination. The Truth of Suffering (duḥkha-satya) produced [thereby] also has two kinds:
namely, the conditioned Truth of Suffering and the unconditioned Truth of Suffering. As the *Ratnagotravibhāga* states: "What is called the 'world' (loka)?"
Because the three realms are like a similar reflection, what is the meaning clarified here?
One should know that within the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*) there are three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*). Their cause is produced by untainted roots of goodness;
therefore, they are called "worldly" because they are dharmas produced apart from tainted karma and afflictions, and they are also called "nirvāṇa. Based on this meaning, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states:
It is said that there is the conditioned world and the unconditioned world, as well as conditioned nirvāṇa and unconditioned nirvāṇa;
therefore, within the karma that can initiate [rebirth], there are also two kinds: first, the ground of abiding ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*), which can initiate and draw forth karma;

second, the habitual tendencies of craving and grasping (*tṛṣṇā-upādāna-vāsanā*), which can give rise to the ground of abiding ignorance. This is why it can initiate the karma that leads to the cycle of birth and death.
Because of this ignorance, one is deluded regarding the nature of one's own mind, which is fundamentally without arousal and ultimately without change.
By the power of these conditions, one is capable of initiating karma that brings about the birth-and-death of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the *manomaya-kāya*.

When a Bodhisattva perceives the Path, they are forever free from subject and object and partially penetrate the fact that there is fundamentally no arousal; therefore, although ignorance still exists, it does not result in the production of [rebirth].
The karma that produces rebirth, by virtue of this power, causes the subsequent paths of expedient means (*upāyamārga*) and so forth to likewise fail to constitute karma that induces rebirth.

For example, although the innate view of self (*sahaja-ātman-dṛṣṭi*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) persist after the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) of the two vehicles, they cannot constitute karma for a collective retribution (*nikāya-sabhāga-vipāka*).
One should know that the principle here is the same; this is why the habituation of the grasping at a person (*pudgala-grāha*) [is not a cause of rebirth].
The conceptualization of grasping at the reality of dharmas (*dharmābhiniveśa-vikalpa*) cannot give rise to this untainted karma (*anāsrava-karman*).

While this principle does not fail to apply to the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), for a Bodhisattva on the path of skillful means (*upāyamārga*), it is cultivated as an antidote to that [grasping]; because the cultivation of untainted karma acts as a counteragent to the characteristics of that grasping, the same applies here.
The ground where ignorance dwells (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*) cannot be subdued or extinguished by untainted karma; therefore, it is able to...
Because such ignorance gives rise to the uncontaminated projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karma*) of all three vehicles, it is specifically designated as the "expedient means" (*upāya*).
At the time of generating karma, it is able to moisten that karma and give rise to the seeds of the grasper (*grāhaka*), thereby enabling the manifestation of uncontaminated karma.
For this reason, the habitual tendencies of craving and grasping (*tṛṣṇā-upādāna-vāsanā*) and the conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*) are able to give rise [to such karma].

Regarding "projecting karma" (*ākṣepaka-karma*), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that non-retrogressive (*avaivartika*) bodhisattvas, by the power of their residual impressions (*vāsanā*), receive a body born of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā-upapatti-deha*). This clarifies the meaning of projecting karma. The *Ratnagotravibhāga* says:

"The 'conditioned aspect' refers to the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-āvasthā*) acting as a condition for formative forces (*saṃskāra*); just as ignorance conditions formative forces, so it is here. This explains the meaning of inducing karma (*āvāhaka-karma*).

Furthermore, that treatise states: "Conditioned by that *avidyā-vāsabhūmi* (ground of the dwelling of ignorance), and with the subtle conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) of habitual tendencies as the cause, untainted karma (*anāsrava-karman*) gives rise to the mental phenomena (*manodharma*). This passage clearly reveals the two types of origination.

Next, regarding the power of linking rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*), when Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas undergo birth, the habitual tendencies of self-love (*ātma-sneha-vāsanā*) remain in the state of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and effect the linking of rebirth.

If the continuity of rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*) induced by the power of a bodhisattva’s wisdom does not require *vāsanā* (habitual tendencies), then in this context, both the linking of rebirth and the production of karma constitute the functional capacity of the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), as these are all contained within the six defilements (*ṣaḍ-rāga*).

Furthermore, that which induces and leads [rebirth] is the power of the ignorance-ground (*avidyā-āvasthā-bhūmi*), which is the obstacle of wisdom (*jñeyāvaraṇa*); since it is not among the six defilements, this obstacle of wisdom exists separately.
There are two kinds of extraordinary functions: first, this ignorance moves True Suchness (tathatā) so that it flows through birth and death, as the Sūtra says:
"This very Dharmakāya flows through the five paths and is called sentient beings"; the *Awakening of Faith* states:
"The intrinsically pure mind, because it is moved by the wind of ignorance... Second, this ignorance can permeate (vāsana) True Suchness, transforming and giving rise to [the phenomenal world].
Regarding all consciousnesses and so forth, as stated in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*: "Inconceivable perfuming and inconceivable transformation constitute the manifesting consciousness.
According to this treatise: "The pure dharma of true thusness (*tathatā*) is in reality free from defilement;

however, because it is perfumed by ignorance, it possesses the appearance of defilement. Thus, due to these two kinds of power, it can serve as the basis for the two kinds of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).

As the *Bhāryāsūtra* states: "The birth of these three stages and those three types of mind-made bodies (*manomayakāya*), as well as birth from untainted karma (*anāsravakarma*), all depend upon the ground of the abiding of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*);
they have conditions and are not without conditions. Therefore, one should know that the power of ignorance is exceptionally superior, as it is said in verse:
"The power of Prajñā is most supreme; it can reach the state of non-action while there is nothing it does not do."

Among all forms of birth and death, the power of ignorance is the greatest; it is able to move the single dharma-realm and universally produce the various gateways of the two types of birth and death.
A detailed analysis of these distinctions is found in the "Chapter on the Two Obstructions" by Master Kuiji.

Eighth, regarding the section on establishing the similarities and differences among the stages: in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, five stages are established. Specifically, the four stages beginning with "Faith" (*śraddhā*) constitute the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-mārga*).
Following the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*), the four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) are separately established as the stage of application (*prayoga-mārga*).

The two types of true and apparent paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) are termed the stage of penetration (*prativedha-mārga*). All remaining stages are termed the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). As for the Buddha...

The stage of fruition (*phala-avasthā*) constitutes the ultimate path (*niṣṭhā-mārga*). Furthermore, the stages of Equal Enlightenment (*samatā-bodhi*) and Wondrous Enlightenment (*vimala-bodhi*) are likewise considered ultimate.

Nevertheless, even prior to these stages (*bhūmi-pūrva*), there are the forty minds, because the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) also constitute formal stages. Thus, the ninth fascicle of that treatise asks:

"What are the five stages for entering into the realization of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*)? First is the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), which refers to cultivating the Mahāyāna factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣa-bhāgīya*)."

Second, the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*) refers to the cultivation of the Mahāyāna aids to penetration (*nirvedha-bhāgīya*). Third, the stage of thorough realization (*prativedha-avasthā*) refers to the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*) wherein all bodhisattvas abide.
Fourth, the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*) refers to the path of meditation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) wherein all bodhisattvas abide.

Fifth, the stage of culmination (*niṣṭhā-avasthā*) refers to abiding in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*); thus the characteristics of these stages are explained in detail. However, regarding the basis of the Mahāyāna and so forth, they are one.

Following the judgment of various masters regarding these five stages, they are categorized as four types of non-retrogression: first, the sixth stage of the Ten Faiths is termed "non-retrogression of faith," because it is called the "mind of non-retrogression";
second, from the seventh stage of the Ten Abidings upward is termed "non-retrogression of position," because one no longer gives rise to false views;
third, from the first Bhūmi upward is termed "non-retrogression of realization," because one has realized the true principle.
From the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, they are called "non-retrogressive in practice" because their practice is effortless (*anābhoga*). However, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"If bodhisattvas dwell in the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), it is called 'inferior accomplishment. If they dwell in the stage of pure superior intention (*śuddhādhyāśaya-bhūmi*), it is called 'middling accomplishment.
If they dwell in the stages from 'certainty' (*niyata*) up to the ultimate (*niṣṭhā-gamana*), it is called 'superior accomplishment. If a bodhisattva...
Even while abiding in the stage of inferior accomplishment, one may still go to evil destinies; this lasts for the entirety of the first asaṃkhyeya kalpa, as explained at length in the treatise.

Based on this textual passage, Xiangxiang (Gandhahastin) judged that it is also possible to generally describe the stages prior to the Bodhisattva-bhūmi as "retrogression," because [at those stages] one still falls into the various evil destinies.
Furthermore, according to the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*, it is only when a bodhisattva reaches the tenth stage of Dedication (*daśamī-pratipatti*) that they [become irreversible].
Question: If that is so, why is the sixth stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) called the "Non-retrogressive Mind" (*avaivartika-citta*)? Answer: The *Xiangxiang Huayan Mingnanji Hui* states:
"Because the non-retrogression of thought has not yet been fully realized, it is merely termed the 'Non-retrogressive Mind'. Question:

If that is so, why does the *Qixin Lun* (Treatise on the Awakening of Faith) state that those from the ten understandings (*daśa-nirvedha-bhūmi*) upward are all called "non-retrogressive"? Answer: [The former refers to] the non-retrogression of intention; [the latter refers to] the actualization of the path. Thus, there is no contradiction.

Answer: Because the two treatises differ in their depth and shallowness of doctrine, the details will be explained below. Regarding the aspects of practice within those stages, as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*:
"When a bodhisattva abiding in the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*) proceeds, what are their practices and what are their characteristics?
At times they possess wisdom and are able to receive, uphold, and so forth all dharmas; at other times they are not able to do so," and so on, up to the full extent of the passage.

It is taught that those who have at one time already resolved their minds toward great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*) but subsequently fall away from it, and others of this same class, are called those dwelling in the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-vihāra*).
Within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), from the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) up to the seventh stage, there are two types of roots:

for Bodhisattvas of gradual awakening (*anupūrva-abhisamaya*), wisdom (*jñāna*) is predominant; for Bodhisattvas of sudden awakening (*sakṛt-abhisamaya*), compassion (*karuṇā*) is predominant. This [continues] up to the eighth stage.

Since, as stated above, those in the two higher stages possess the nature of non-duality, and because their compassion and wisdom are equal and function without effort (*anābhoga*), a question arises:

If from the eighth stage upward, the mind of untainted contemplation (*anāsrava-bhāvanā-citta*) in which compassion and wisdom are equal continues at all times, how can it be said that there is "leaping over kalpas"?
For example, at the beginning of the third kalpa, Śākyamuni Buddha encountered Dīpaṃkara Buddha; by spreading his hair to cover the mud, he leaped over eight kalpas. How is this to be understood?

Having completed three *kalpas* of cultivation for the marks of a Buddha, he first encountered the Buddha Vipasyin (勝觀佛) and also the Buddha Puṣya (弗沙); by standing on one foot in praise, he surpassed nine *kalpas*.

Regarding this, Master Huizhao of the Tang dynasty briefly preserved two interpretations: the first says that there may be a certain class of beings who dwell frequently in the mind of contemplative wandering (*yòuguān xīn*), or who are long addicted to the meditative absorption of cessation (*nièdìng*, *nirodha-samāpatti*);
in contrast to these, there is "surpassing" [the time required]. If this is so, how is it that those from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward [attain Buddhahood] without such surpassing?
Question: Does it increase and progress moment by moment? Answer: This is stated in reference to the long duration following the entry, stay, and exit from the eighth bhūmi and above.
Question: If that is so, how can it be said that from the first bhūmi upward, the minds of entry, stay, and exit are each equal?

Answer: If one refers to the application of attention (*manasikāra*), then their functional power is equal; this is not the case prior to the bhūmis, for when applying attention there, the power and function are unequal.
